items.title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines
items.author: luu
items.content:
classic approach is a fan in a box, though in the past ten years people have mostly switched over to electronic ones. But a fan is really a great approach; you just need to put it to better use: have the fan clean the air.

Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, here's a $47 purifier with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning 34 cubic feet of air per minute ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.

Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an AirFanta 3Pro and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.

Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

items.title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
items.author: molind
items.content:
We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip, under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.

A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, :

Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.

Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.

A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:

While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. and the edge flips to BD; and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins.

"Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.

Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 302 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.

An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.

Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or :

The triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive means a convex corner:

A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.

Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.

The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around:

the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. the sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.

Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.

The naive clipper (−1,812 ms)​

With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row:

is shorter than in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.

Test only the dents (−237 ms)​

Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a . So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.

The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:

The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.

Skip tests on convex polygons (−2 ms)​

A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:

The turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The passes; the star changes direction four times, at the corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.

The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.

So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:

The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:

When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.

Sort the dents into buckets (−65 ms)​

A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.

Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: .

Count without branches (−178 ms)​

The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:

The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.

Test only the marked dents (−30 ms)​

When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:

Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.

Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście, a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour:

per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.

When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.

Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.

The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; in C++ and in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.

Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut, the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:

WebAssembly, loop inside the module, V8 / JSC
WebAssembly, one call from JS per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, one call per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, direct calls, all polygons in one call, V8 / JSC

Natively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.

The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.

Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.

earstrip is on GitHub and npm, with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.

items.title: Feds suspect ransom negotiator ran ShinyHunters extortion site
items.author: Bender
items.content:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect . Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for , an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against , the former chief executive of , a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called . He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: . In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address .

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address  is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “ has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the , a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired , a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company , stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate , 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

is chief executive at , an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ chargedMonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

items.title: Academics have a duty to defend open knowledge systems like Wikipedia
items.author: jruohonen
items.content:
Despite being the most widely consulted reference work ever created Wikipedia faces existential challenges from generative AI companies whose products divert traffic away from it. argues academics, by virtue of their responsibilities as researchers and teachers in higher education, have an ethical duty to defend and support open knowledge communities such as Wikipedia.

When people use AI products like Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT, they are treated to immediate answers. Sometimes such answers include links to Wikipedia. However, most users of AI products do not click the links to Wikipedia, choosing instead to accept machine-generated outputs without further verification. If this practice continues, readership on Wikipedia will continue to decline.

The AI threat to Wikipedia

This is a problem for Wikipedia because it is run by a volunteer community that does everything from writing, coding, and administration, and this community comes from Wikipedia’s readers. A decline in the number of readers means fewer articles, updates, and corrections – and ultimately, a derelict and quite possibly defunct encyclopedia. This would be a loss for humanity as well as for the AI industry itself, as it is heavily reliant upon Wikipedia and its five billion words for training the systems that run their products.

Wikipedia, of course, is more than training data for machines; it is a self-governing community of people that exists independently of commercial or governmental controls. This community of volunteers exists to produce and share knowledge for the common good. It is difficult to think of any other volunteer endeavour that has been more influential, pervasive, and powerful than Wikipedia. It has been more successful than commercial enterprises like Microsoft’s encyclopedia, Encarta and xAI’s machine-generated Grokipedia, and it is perceived to be so influential that it has been banned in some countries, like China.

However, the powerful AI companies that now control online search pose existential challenges for a weakened and demoralised community, as in addition to stripping Wikipedia of readers, they have misappropriated the hard work of volunteers for their own profit, reducing writing and research to machine feed. Some AI companies take Wikipedia’s content through unauthorised scraping, while others, including Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta, pay Wikipedia for high-speed API access to its pages.

Academia’s duty to protect open knowledge

Academia’s duty to protect open knowledge like that produced on Wikipedia is grounded in its privileged position within and structural connection to knowledge. According to Iris Marion Young’s Social Connection Model, one’s duty to remedy injustice is determined by one’s connection to processes and structures in which one participates. As a participant in knowledge processes, academia has a responsibility to address injustices in those processes – such as those committed by the AI industry against vital sources of knowledge like Wikipedia.

With its access to resources and higher status than the largely anonymous group of Wikipedia volunteers, academia has the power and influence to address the injustice of an endangered Wikipedia, as well as the capacity to do so. As people who are trained in producing knowledge and who teach the next generation of knowledge producers, academics are in fact uniquely qualified to support Wikipedia’s current and future reserves of knowledge, as well as its community of volunteers.

How can academics support Wikipedia?

Academics are not the ones that have harmed Wikipedia, they – as fellow stewards of knowledge – have a duty to help defend it from those that have. And academics are well-equipped to do so; their subject matter expertise can be used to address content gaps, correct errors, and provide context on complicated topics on Wikipedia. Academics’ access to and facility with high-quality sources can help improve Wikipedia’s quality. And as Wikipedia’s citation practices mirror those academic practices, academics may find editing Wikipedia to be less daunting than others do.

Along with contributing their expertise and knowledge to Wikipedia’s pages, academics can also support Wikipedia by integrating it into their scholarly work. Just as academics must cite any AI-generated machine outputs they rely upon in their research and writing, they can also cite Wikipedia if they use it in their work. Doing so can highlight Wikipedia’s value to other academics as a source of knowledge and provide greater transparency in one’s research processes. Despite longstanding skepticism of Wikipedia among some scholars, citations to Wikipedia in academic journals appear to be increasing – even in high-impact publications in subject areas like the health sciences.

Academics can also support Wikipedia by teaching their students how to contribute to Wikipedia. This practice can enhance knowledge and understanding about Wikipedia among future generations and has the added benefits of helping students bolster their subject matter knowledge and information literacy skills. Many instructors are already supporting Wikipedia in this way. Through the non-profit Wiki Education Foundation, more than 152,000 students at over 8,000 colleges and universities in the United States and Canada have contributed more than 125 million words to Wikipedia since 2010.

Students report that writing for Wikipedia provides them with motivation to produce high-quality writing, as they are writing for a real-world audience. Students also develop practicalinformation literacy skills in source evaluation, copyright compliance, and source attribution. In addition, because Wikipedia currently bansAI-generated writing, instructors may find assigning Wikipedia work to be one way for students to build writing and thinking skills independently. As about 19% of Wikipedia’s new active editors come from Wiki Education’s programs, teaching students to contribute to Wikipedia is a viable way to sustain and renew it with a new generation of contributors.

The fulfilment of ethical obligations to support knowledge communities, however, requires support from institutions of higher education. Currently, most academics are evaluated on their scholarly and research achievements, teaching performance, and service duties to their departments. Public service, like contributing to Wikipedia, goes largely unrecognised, if it is even counted at all. If academics are to fulfil their responsibilities to protect knowledge and knowledge communities, institutions must recognise efforts like contributing to Wikipedia and provide resources and support. Doing so may also help to address the public’s eroding trust in higher education itself, as a greater commitment to serving the public would reassert the role of universities as stewards of knowledge that exist to serve humanity – a role shared by Wikipedia.

items.title: What shall I teach my son?
items.author: Curiositry
items.content:
What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI?

October 19, 2026 · Discussion on HN

Yesterday, the title by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father.

My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?

Mr. Edison says That the radio will supplant the teacher.

Already one may learn languages by means

Of Victrola records.

The moving picture will visualize

What the radio fails to get across.

Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods.

With fire-horses, Or, perhaps shown in museums.

Education will become a matter

Of pressing the button.

Perhaps I can get a position at the switchboard.

– Quoted in by Neil Postman, quoting Teachers and Machines: The Use of Technology Since 1920 by Larry Cuban

Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools… Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.

Back in 2013, I boldly predicted that MOOCs would upend education. Ah, my past self, you sweet summer child.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has helped me appreciate the staying power of staying power, sometimes called The Lindy Effect. Merely staying alive implies some anti-fragility to adapt and survive. Consider that Harvard, Yale, and Princeton were founded to educate the clergy. From

In the Western world, beginning in the thirteenth century and for five hundred years afterward, that God was sufficient justification for the founding of institutions of learning, from grammar schools, where children were taught to read the Bible, to great universities, where men were trained to be ministers of God.

Schools survived what happened to religion. It should be no surprise that they’ve survived the radio, motion pictures, and the internet.

We typically confuse why something claims it exists, ie to glorify God, vs the forces that actually perpetuate it, which are subtler, we’d prefer not spoken aloud, and more prosaic, ie endowments, prestige, and needing someone to watch one’s kids.

It has been a surprisingly good bet that schools will continue to exist in roughly their current form for many years to come. Ironically, there also seems to be some staying power to technologists boldly (and so far incorrectly) doubting the staying power of schools! I myself have contributed to this grand tradition multiple times, and find myself at risk of doing it yet again.

Surely this time must finally be different, right? We have captured intelligence in a bottle, and you’re telling me that “Ok class, turn to page 17” and “Does anyone know how to solve for x” are still going to be around in the 2030s?

There are many shifting purposes to education, which underpin how it has survived this long. As the times change, so do its purposes shift and adapt, such as:

    I once tried to come up with a single-word purpose for education, and I landed upon the word “resourceful”, because I reasoned that if you “were able to use arbitrary resources to uncover and solve problems”, you had no more need for schooling. In the age of Google, email, and the internet, a person was educated when they could wield them. But now I see my vision of resourcefulness perfected in the AI agent and its tool loop. Maybe resourcefulness will go the way of the Dewey Decimal System which in turn supplanted memorization and an oral tradition.

    Imagine education as a table held up by its many purposes. I didn’t realize how centrally important “the ability to earn a living” was for me until it started to wobble. A big reason is because I’m looking for a more objective arbiter of “good” in education. Education’s own tests and measures can feel stifling. The market offered a counterpoint. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates were college dropouts, but the market deemed them good. Now that I think of it, apparently Einstein was a mediocre student, but his contributions to science were his way out. With recent advances in AI mathematics, both of these paths to glory are under fire. Clara Collier makes similar points in her exceptional essay “After Work, We’ll Have Each Other.”

    If AI takes our ability to contribute, what’s left for our children?

    Neil Postman offers a few suggestions for positive purposes for education that I found heartening, not mainly for their content, but for the fact that it’s possible to make up new purposes for education and advocate for them. My favorite suggestions of Postman’s are:

    • Spaceship Earth – we’re all in this together; let’s take care of each other and our planet

    • The American Experiment – let’s revive our sense of wonder, curiosity, and responsibility about what America is and can be

    • The World Makers – as a student of McLuhan, Postman would be remiss if he didn’t invite students to make the tools and narratives that thereafter make us

    At the risk of going too meta, I do strongly believe in Postman’s point (in his other education book, Teaching as a Subversive Activity) that “the medium is the message.” That the we teach what we teach is often more important than the . And likewise, I believe in Dr. Alfie Kohn’s notion that we should relate to our educational charges as humans, not objects – “doing with” vs “doing to”. Thus, I believe it may be most honest and effective to invite our children to help us craft the purpose for their education as we figure it out together.

The “Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon” is a game where players try to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon in fewer than six steps, where each step links two actors who co-starred in a film.

The conventional wisdom is that Kevin Bacon is the all-encompassing center of Hollywood, so prolific that the game is a lot easier than if it were called the “Six Degrees of John Doe.”

Samuel L. Jackson is the , with a remoteness of just 2.09. Willem Dafoe is second at 2.13, and Robert De Niro follows at 2.14.

Women are underrepresented among the top 100, taking only 16 spots. Nicole Kidman is the highest-ranking woman at #21.

Let’s create a time machine for the center of Hollywood and calculate actors’ remoteness in previous years. Our time machine starts at the end of 2025.

Let’s time travel to 2006, when Samuel L. Jackson took the crown.

Kevin Bacon still does not appear; his highest rank was #108 in 1996 after his role in “Sleepers.”

We can view all centers of Hollywood since 1980. Use the slider to look around.

How might we predict who will take the crown from Samuel L. Jackson? Let’s apply this idea to the .

To do that, we need to find what affects an actor’s remoteness score.

One obvious metric is film count. Indeed, Samuel L. Jackson appeared in far more films than anyone else in our 169,000 actor dataset. Nicolas Cage, who’s the next closest, appeared in 96 films.

While the relationship between film count and remoteness is strong, it doesn't fully explain actors’ scores. For example, Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick differ significantly in their remoteness, despite appearing in the same number of films.

The difference between Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick lies in their co-stars: Natalie Portman is cast in films with more prolific actors than Anna Kendrick. Of the 250 most-connected actors, Natalie Portman has worked with almost three times as many as Anna Kendrick has.

So if you work with more “big dog” actors compared to someone with the same film count, you'll almost certainly be closer to the center of Hollywood. Consequently, co-star film count is the next important factor: this is an actor’s 50 most prolific co-stars by number of films, taken as an average.

Test your knowledge with a few examples: for these actors with similar film counts, who do you think works with more “big dogs” and is more connected to all of Hollywood?

We now have everything we need to predict the future Samuel L. Jackson using film count and co-star data. Our contenders are 99 actors born since 1997 (i.e., Gen Z) who have appeared in at least 5 films.

For the prediction, we need to model actors’ film count and co-star trajectory. To do this, we look at what has happened to actors with similar data in the past.

When predicting film count, consider Sydney Sweeney, who has appeared in 16 films since her debut 15 years ago. By the same point in his career, Robert De Niro also racked up 16 films, and he went on to have a brilliant career totalling 87. By contrast, Chevy Chase reached the same 16-film milestone, but ultimately only appeared in 27 total.

Conversely, after 47 years in Hollywood, Kevin Bacon has a similar film count to Helen Mirren and Gene Hackman.

You'll remember Gene Hackman from the time machine; Kevin Bacon could have been the center of Hollywood if he were born 20 years earlier.

To model a Gen Z actor’s trajectory, we consider comparable careers based on film count and career age, randomly selecting one weighted by similarity.

By applying the same approach for co-star film count, we can start predicting.

To achieve a stable result, we'll run the simulation 10,000 times and see who comes out on top.

The most wins across the 10,000 simulations:

    Chloë Grace Moretz is the most likely Samuel L. Jackson for Gen Z, winning over 10% of simulations. It’s by no means a landslide: her median remoteness is 2.19 and median projected film count is 66, quite far from Samuel L. Jackson’s stratospheric numbers of 116 career films and a 2.09 remoteness score.

    As time goes on, Samuel L. Jackson will eventually stop appearing in films and have fewer connections to new actors, lowering his remoteness score.

    Meanwhile, younger actors will continue starring in films and overtake his status as the center of Hollywood. What we don’t know, however, is exactly how long that will take.

This is IKEA's manual for the , with a 3D model that builds it step by step. Each step starts from the drawing's angle, and you can turn it around to see the rest.

Two sides, a top, a bottom, a fixed shelf, a plinth, four shelves and a back that comes folded in three. Plus 82 pieces of hardware: 16 dowels, 12 cam screws, 12 cam locks, 18 nails, 16 shelf pins and two wall brackets with their screws and washers. The cyan outline on the wall is the finished bookcase.

A cam screw goes into the side with its head sticking out. When a board goes on, the head drops into a round in the board. Give the cam half a turn clockwise and a ramp inside it pulls the head in, clamping the boards together. items.title: My Friend Bob Cringely
items.author: zinxq
items.content:
In 1996, I was a Ph.D. student at Syracuse University. One evening I was sitting in my office and the phone rang,

“Hello?” “Is this Paul Tyma?”

Bob replied in very fast English. “This is Bob Cringely. I just read 7 Java books and yours is the best.”

My first thought was “Huh. He actually said my last name correctly”.

But my quick 2nd thought was that there were not, in fact, 7 Java books in existence. I did indeed write a Java book, but to my knowledge, mine was the 2nd on the market and even then, I’m not sure it was the best. My Ph.D. advisor, Doug Lea, had been an early member of the Java project at Sun Microsystems. He introduced Java (and the JVM) to all his grad students and I believe something like 4 of us wrote books piggybacking upon the hype at the time.

In any case, as you might know, it is not common to get accolades or even much attention for writing a programming book. I had no idea who this “Bob Cringely” person was, but, um, Thanks! So glad you liked it - let’s talk some more about how great it is!

I didn’t know it then, but Bob was way ahead of me. It’s likely he pictured me as some lonely computer geek (or “nerd” in his parlance) sitting in a tiny office tip-tapping away at some code enjoying yesterday’s pizza. (He was right). He also knew computer nerds like me were typically a bit starved for attention, especially around anything related to computer-centric achievements. Again, Bob knew his audience.

He continued, “Do you do Java programming too?”

Writing a programming book in the 1990’s afforded many of the same benefits as today. In other words, nearly nothing. You sure weren’t getting rich off writing books. But it did get me invites to teach Java at some Software Conferences. Which then got me invites to train Java to teams inside different companies. Because of that, my friend and I started a company around Java training. We hadn’t done any contract programming until then, but we’d talked about it plenty.

“Sure we do!”, I rather lied.

From there, Bob hired us to build him a system called (or codenamed?) “Pronto”.

Pronto was to be the distribution future of print Magazines. The big idea was for customers (who were paper magazine subscribers) to install a small daemon process on their computer that would monitor for times where their Internet connection (i.e. often dialup modem at this point) was online but mostly idle. Our system would then slowly but persistently download their next month’s issue of “Good Housekeeping” or “Car and Driver””. Once it was fully downloaded, the daemon would lie in wait until 2am the next morning and send the PDF off to their home printer. The customer would wake up to be happily surprised by a fully printed copy of their magazine waiting for them!

Like many at the time, Bob didn’t believe that reading online would replace reading a full-color, paper magazine. But how that magazine got to your house could change, and that’s where Pronto came in.

Bob had secured funding for Pronto - from someone in Japan I think. I don’t remember, but I remember Bob paid us consistently for the time it took to develop Pronto. After we finished, I don’t know what happened to Pronto, except that it never released in any meaningful sense. But this did begin my 30-year relationship with Bob (or “Cringe” as we called him).

As I said, before this, I had no idea who Bob was. I didn’t know about his claim-to-fame book “Accidental Empires”. His PBS series “Triumph of the Nerds” was released right around the time I was working with/for him. Well after Pronto somehow I got put on Bob’s list of “People I’m going to send my next startup idea to for thoughts” email list. I was by no means alone on that list, and sometimes I got into email threads with some interesting Tech personalities.

I just took a look - and I have had 320 emails with Bob in the past 13 years. Mind you, those aren’t unique emails, most are part of long email chains so I’d estimate I’d email with Bob about 3 times a year since the late 90’s.

Usually, the email chains started with Bob emailing me a wall-of-text about his new startup idea. While the first half of the email was about the idea, invariably, the 2nd half was about how much money it was going to make. I was always impressed at how “to the penny” he got with his projections for something that was basically an idea written on a virtual napkin.

Some ideas were good, and some were not so good. Through my career, I actually joined him in 2 ventures - home-account and Sonisafe. I have the pitch decks for a few, and the detailed descriptions of a bunch more ideas that maybe no one else has seen. This was a great honor in the beginning, especially as his fame grew. But all along the way, I felt Bob was missing the point.

If you ever met Bob - or heck, just saw him in any of his TV specials, you could see Bob charmed everyone he met. He was good-looking, disarming, and curious. He was also an excellent writer, but it was on the screen where he really shined. He was comforting and fun to watch. He was fearless and made people feel special. He wasn’t a “nerd” but if, like me, you were; he understood you and he made it OK. In fact, at times, he even made it look glamorous.

Bob changed people’s lives. His love for Technology was contagious and he inspired a lot of people to pursue a career in Tech. Reading his obituary comments gave me a renewed appreciation for his influence.

Despite his innumerable gifts, Bob seemed to really want to be a superstar startup founder. I’m sure if one of his startup ideas had exploded, Bob would have filled the role fine. But to me - he was a pure natural in front of the camera. I always thought he should start a Youtube channel interviewing Silicon Valley celebrities. I sent him a few emails along those lines, but Bob would mostly just ignore me. He was usually too excited about his new/current startup idea.

When I lived in San Francisco, he and I had lunch or dinner occasionally. He really was a Silicon Valley celebrity. When the inevitable person(s) would come up to him telling them they were a huge fan, he’d act like it was the first time anyone ever recognized him. Every time. The TV Cringe instantly came to life and it was always a pleasure to watch.

Goodbye Mr. Cringely. I’m very sorry to see you go. I will miss you.

A few more Cringe stories

Right after the C# language was released (it must have been around 2001 or so?), I spent the evening and into the morning reading about it. Finally around 2am, with bleary eyes and a racing mind I emailed Bob - “Dotnet is going to squish Java”.

I got a response 2 minutes later, “Why?”.

I spent the next hour writing an overly long and terribly rough email, in a half-awake, caffeine-induced state and sent it off. I woke up the next morning to Bob’s new blog post - a rather lightly edited version of my rant!

I just remember being grateful he didn’t mention me. But then he called me later that day, “Sun is a bit unhappy with the blog post. I’ve been summoned to Sun Headquarters tomorrow and you’re coming with me.”

The next day Bob and I went to Sun Microsystems. He and I sat in a room with Jonathan Schwartz (CEO) and Rich Greene (C-something-else) while they defended Java and gave me nasty looks wondering who the hell I was and why the hell I was even there. They seemed plenty interested in impressing Bob though. By the way, Dotnet didn’t squish Java but I did get a Sun T-shirt.

After that, Whenever I emailed him, I often tacked onto the bottom of my emails - “Do whatever you want with this email, but don’t mention me. And know this email could be totally wrong or silly - either way, it’s yours now”.

In and around 2004 I was living in NYC and I got a forwarded email from Bob. It was a forward from a Producer at the TV network VH1 telling him they were doing a video series called “My Coolest Years” and had a special episode about “Geeks” and they needed a computer geek. They asked him if he wanted to be interviewed about what it was like being a “geek” in high school.

He replied to the Producer, cc’ing me:

“Sorry, but I got laid plenty in high school. However, I have cc’d my friend Paul who actually was a geek in high school. He also lives in NYC.”

Continuing the the theme of Bob getting me into places I probably didn’t belong, I ended up with a total of about 8 minutes in the show alongside Mark Cuban, John Tesh, Ben Stein, and Wil Wheaton. Bob would have been way better.

Randomly, a few months ago I once again watched Bob’s “Plane Crazy.” A classic. And because of the comments surrounding his death I found that his special “The Transformation Age” is also on Youtube which I had never seen (in 8 or so separate videos). It’s quintessential Cringe.

items.title: Lula supporters protest against Meta to denounce its 'electoral interference'
items.author: jumpocelot
items.content:
São Paulo (EFE).- Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva protested outside the São Paulo headquarters of tech giant Meta on Monday, six days before the election. They accused the company of favoring content from opposition candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

Organized by the platform «Não Se Meta,» the protest drew about 200 demonstrators who demanded that the company, led by Mark Zuckerberg, explain its actions.

The protesters accused Meta of «interfering in the elections and harming President Lula by reducing the reach of his posts and boosting those of Flavio.»

«Meta cannot be an invisible judge of the electoral process,» they argued outside the company’s Brazil headquarters, accusing it of committing electoral crimes since the 2018 election, when Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2023) became president.

On Monday, the Superior Electoral Court gave Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, 24 hours to demonstrate that it guarantees equal treatment for the campaigns of the two candidates for the Planalto Palace.

Both Lula and Bolsonaro have filed complaints with the electoral court, alleging that their political content is disadvantaged on Meta’s platforms. The company has denied any interference in the elections.

One of the rally’s goals was to demand that the tech giant stop «manipulating elections through social media» and «preventing content aimed at the working class from reaching them.»

Protesters denounced the removal or reduction of content, noting that it impacts public debate and the balance of the electoral contest. They also noted that 70% of the Brazilian population gets its news from Instagram.

«Digital sovereignty is no joke. It’s something that must be taken very seriously,» declared Veronyka Gimenes, an activist known on social media as Trava Hacker.

According to Gimenes, companies like Meta are part of a “digital colonialism” project that aims to dominate countries like Brazil and experiment with their electoral processes.

«In Lula’s fourth term, we will achieve autonomy with our own social media platforms, open and transparent,» said fellow activist Tiana Cauton. She added that «we must take to the streets for the right to communication.»

«Big Tech is part of the hate industry that has blood on its hands,» claimed Mandi Coelho, an activist who traveled to Gaza with the Global Sumud Flotilla.

While holding banners and signs featuring photos of Zuckerberg and United States President Donald Trump, attendees chanted: “Digital sovereignty! Meta out of the electoral process!” EFE

items.title: Putting Linux on my RTX Spark laptop because I don't have a Microsoft account
items.author: pfeifferj
items.content:
tl;dr - boo hoo microsoft bad. Arch Linux works, keeps up with Windows in 7-Zip, and reports the same 116.0 GiB memory pool to the OS and CUDA. My initial bootable setup and patches are here. This is for the ASUS ProArt P16 H7607BA-SE033W: the 128 GB RAM configuration with 6,144 CUDA cores and a 2 TB SSD.

When rumours started circulating about a laptop with over 100 GiB of RAM the GPU could access, I started thinking about all the things I could build on it and all the optimisations I could spend far too long playing with. I'm very pro open-weight models. Being able to run things locally and mess around with RL, quantisation and fine-tuning on a laptop would be sick. I already publish my own GGUF quants on Hugging Face, with over 160,000 downloads in the past month.

NVIDIA has been doing kernel work for Ubuntu, which gave me a starting point. I incorporated that, fixed the ACPI override allocation and framebuffer mapping needed to get a console, and worked out the ACPI overrides from the laptop's own tables (thanks astra <3). The NVIDIA driver and ASUS speaker firmware came from official places on the internet (pls don't sue me computer companies). Keyboard support needed a patched , and audio needed its own machine driver.

I put this together into a bootable USB and extended upstream Archinstall 4.5 to install the hardware support. The repo has the build scripts and patches, including the steps to dump your own ACPI tables and extract the speaker firmware from ASUS's driver package locally. Mine runs firmware H7607BA.300.

The build inputs are hash pinned. The hardware packages I put together over the weekend are signed with my Arch Linux Package Maintainer key, and the ACPI overrides come from the laptop itself.

The display runs at 3840 × 2400 and 120 Hz, and I use NetworkManager, PipeWire, and rootless Podman with NVIDIA CDI. The installer holds the kernel, NVIDIA, power-management and firmware packages with , while ordinary packages keep updating from Arch Linux ARM.

I ran the suite on October 19 on native Arch Linux ARM, with kernel and NVIDIA driver . The laptop was plugged in with the performance profile selected. For the CPU comparison, I used published Windows results.

The CPU test is native ARM64 7-Zip 26.04 with a fixed 32 MiB dictionary. I ran one warmup and three measured passes at each thread count, then took the medians:

Single-thread is basically a tie. With all 20 threads, my Linux setup is about 5% ahead on compression and 3% ahead on decompression. The HP review doesn't specify its 7-Zip version or dictionary size, so these percentages compare the two laptop setups.

ComputerBase also tested a ProArt P16 with the 20-core N1X. Converted to GIPS, its Windows 7-Zip score was 155.774; the median total from my three runs was 157.084. Their result sits inside my three-run range of 155.759 to 157.193 GIPS. Their machine was the 64 GB configuration and ran 7-Zip 26.00, and the chart doesn't give the dictionary size.

With a 91 GiB dedicated reservation, Frandroid's Windows setup reported a CUDA total of 109.7 GiB, including shared memory. My Linux setup reported 116.0 GiB, about 6.3 GiB more. What I care about is having the large pool available for CPU work too, without moving the reservation slider and rebooting between workloads.

I ran NVIDIA's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local checkpoint through vLLM with B12X CUDA kernels in a native ARM64 container, using mixed quantization and FP8 KV cache. I turned off thinking for this run.

Before loading the model, Linux reported 110.9 GiB of available RAM. vLLM logged 68.2 GiB for model loading and allocated another 21.1 GiB to the KV cache. That's nearly 90 GiB allocated to the model and KV cache on a laptop.

Model loading and compilation took about 16 minutes before the first request. The timings below start after warmup. PLE embedding tables are backed by disk and benefit from a warm page cache; other components use CPU offload. CUDA handles inference, with some of the model outside GPU memory.

I gave Qwen two buggy Python helpers to review, a long incident log with one failed operation to find, and a payment note to turn into JSON. Each task ran three times after warmup, with known answers to check against. I wanted to know how long I'd wait and whether it returned the right fields.

The incident task read nearly 10,000 tokens and returned the correct request, cause, and next action in under 6 s. Its answer was only 39 tokens long, which comes to 6.8 tokens/s over the whole request. Most of the wait went into processing the prompt, so for this task the response time tells me more than the tokens/s figure.

Both ProArt setups are around 30 tokens/s. For inference, Frandroid used an 85 GiB dedicated reservation and a context limit of 262,144 tokens; my context limit was 32,768 tokens. The prompts, quants, runtimes, and timing methods differ. This compares two working configurations; it doesn't isolate the effect of the OS.

I also sent four code reviews at once. The median batch finished in 5.314 s, producing 86.6 output tokens/s across all four requests combined. That rate includes prompt processing and response overhead. All 12 answers passed over three batches.

Then I left it cycling through the three tasks, one request at a time, for ten minutes. It finished 150 requests, 50 of each, and every answer passed the checks. Median response times were 4.036 s for code review, 5.921 s for the log, and 2.046 s for extraction. Comparing the first ten and last ten repetitions of each task, median response times grew by less than 1.6%.

All 171 measured responses passed the checks. That's three prompts repeated with deterministic decoding; the code-review check verifies the regression outputs. I kept every answer and raw event stream and checked them against the summaries.

items.title: Dungeon Generation in the Gnomish Mines of NetHack
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
Ok, this one is really best explained with a visualiser:

NetHack’s level generation has a lot of interesting things, but I wanted to focus on the Gnomish Mines because of their use of Cellular Automata. This gives it an organic caves feel, while the majority of the game is spent in square rooms.

It’s very straightforward:

  • Randomly pick 40% of the cells to be floor
  • Apply four passes of Cellular Automata
  • Fix up disconnected caves with extra corridors

Let’s dive into the cellular automata specifically. There’s only two states – floor or rock. And each pass works by counting how many floor tiles are in the 8-neighbor hood of each cell.

Pass 1: 0-2 → rock; 3-4 → unchanged, 5-8 → floorPass 2: 0-4 → unchanged; 5 → rock; 6-8 → unchanged

Pass 3: 0-2 → rock; 3-8 → unchanged.

Pass 4:

Interestingly, pass 1 is unbuffered. Each cell is updated in place before moving to the next cell. All the rest are buffered – all cells have new computed values, then the entire grid updated at once.

Pass 1 creates floors near other floors, and creates rocks near other rocks. I’d call this a “clustering” pass, that pushes the random tiles towards wide open areas of tiles. The unbuffering is important here so that you don’t flop-flop, turning something rock→floor near something turning floor→rock.

Passes 3 and 4 are erosion routines, it’s a very common use of cellular automata. If you have 6-8 rocks nearby, then you also become a rock. That tends to smooth out corners, and delete tiny islands.

Pass 2 though… It turns cells to rock if they have exactly 5 floor neighbors (i.e. 3 rock neighbors). I’m still struggling to understand what purpose this is intended to achieve. Any ideas?
