items.title: The Intel 8087 chip: floating-point addition and subtraction
items.author: pwg
items.content:
In 1980, Intel introduced the 8087, a chip that made floating-point operations much faster in the IBM PC and other systems. Although the 8087 supports advanced operations such as tangents, square roots, and logarithms, this article focuses on basic arithmetic operations: addition and subtraction. The 8087 provided a spectacular speed improvement over the 8086 processor, speeding up addition by a factor of almost 100, and complicated operations by even more. In this article, I examine the 8087's microcode and circuitry to explain exactly how floating-point addition and subtraction are implemented, including numerous special cases for infinities and other special values.

To explore the 8087's circuitry, I popped the lid off a chip with a chisel and used a microscope to create the high-resolution image below. The microcode ROM is the large rectangular region in the center of the die, holding the 1648 micro-instructions that control the chip. The bottom half of the chip (red box) is the datapath, the circuitry that performs floating-point calculations on 80-bit values.

A close-up of the 8087's datapath, showing functional blocks that are used for addition and subtraction. Click this image (or any other) for a larger version.

Zooming in on the datapath shows the functional blocks that are important for addition and subtraction. The key component is the integer adder, located in the center. It receives one argument from the B register and another argument from a component such as the temporary registers or the stack registers. The adder's output is stored in the sum register. The shifter can shift the bits in a value to the left or the right. The shifter occupies a lot of space on the die because its circuitry allows a value to be rapidly shifted by an arbitrary number of bits. Floating-point operations make heavy use of the shifter to align values; the leading zero circuitry counts the number of zero bits or bytes on the left of a value so they can be shifted away. The exponent converter processes exponents, detecting overflows and underflows. These specialized circuits helped the 8087 achieve its high performance.

Floating-point addition and subtraction

Most computers use integers as their basic representation for numbers. But many applications need to use numbers with a fractional part, such as 1.23. Moreover, integers have a very limited range: a 32-bit integer can express numbers from about -2 billion to 2 billion. To solve these problems, computers usually implement floating-point numbers, which provide fractional numbers over an enormous range.

In most cases, a floating-point number is represented by × × 2. The significand is a binary number of the form : a leading 1, followed by the binary point (the binary equivalent of the decimal point) and the rest of the bits. In a binary number, each bit represents a power of 2. For the fractional part, the part after the binary point, the powers of 2 are negative: 2, 2, and so forth. So the binary number 1.1 is 1 + 1/2, or 1.5 in decimal. Similarly, binary 1.0011 is 1 + 1/8 + 1/16 or 1.1875. The exponent allows numbers to escape the limited range of the significand. For instance, 1.1 (binary) × 2 is 384. With larger exponents, floating-point numbers can cover a huge range; even a 32-bit short floating-point number covers a range exceeding 10 to 10.

Floating-point addition and subtraction are more complicated than integer operations. Before the numbers can be added (or subtracted), their binary points must be aligned, the same as aligning the decimal points for decimal numbers. After the operation, the exponent of the result must be adjusted, normalizing the significand so it starts with a 1 bit.

The steps for a simple floating-point addition.

The diagram above illustrates a simple floating-point addition: . The first two lines show the two arguments expressed with an exponent and significand. Both arguments are normalized, so the leftmost bit is a 1. Before adding, the second argument must be aligned—making the exponents equal—by shifting it two positions to the right. (The difference between the exponents in this case is two.) The values are then added, using integer addition on the aligned significands. In this case, adding the values causes an overflow, an "extra" bit on the left. The result must be normalized by shifting it one position to the right and incrementing the exponent by 1.

Floating-point subtraction is similar, but has a few more complications. The result can be positive, negative, or zero. The result can be orders of magnitude smaller than the arguments. The figure below shows a basic subtraction, 8-7.5. As with addition, the second argument is shifted right so the exponents match (i.e., the binary points line up). The two significands are subtracted with integer subtraction. The result is normalized by shifting to the left so the top bit is a 1. Unlike the addition case, normalization may require a large shift. In this case, the shift is four bits and the exponent is decremented by 4 to yield the result.

A simple floating-point subtraction.

One complication with subtraction is that the result can be negative. If that occurs, the significand is made positive, and the sign of the result is flipped. Subtraction can also result in zero. In this case, normalization cannot be performed; instead, a special value +0 or -0 is returned as appropriate.

Relevant hardware details of the 8087

In this section, I'll explain some features of the 8087 that play important roles in the microcode implementation of addition and subtraction.

The 8087 supports a variety of data types, but internally, the 8087 stores numbers in an 80-bit format called "temporary real". A temporary real number has a sign bit, a 15-bit exponent, and a 64-bit significand. The 15-bit exponent allows numbers that are absurdly large, over 10. The 64-bit significand supports extremely accurate numbers. The exponent is stored with a "bias" of 16383 added to it. Thus, the stored exponent is always positive, even if the real exponent is negative. For instance, an exponent of 1 is stored as , and an exponent of -16 is stored as .

The 80-bit temporary real format and the register formats. The dot indicates the binary point, analogous to the decimal point.

The 8087 has eight internal registers, organized as a stack. The programmer uses these registers when programming the 8087. Each register holds an 80-bit floating-point number. To optimize performance, each value in the register stack also has an associated "tag" value: zero, valid, special, or empty. A value of zero is tagged as . A "normal" floating-point value is tagged as . If the value is infinity, Not a Number (NaN), or a denormalized value, then it is tagged as . Finally, an tag indicates that a register does not hold a value; this allows detection of stack underflow (reading an empty register) or stack overflow (storing to a non-empty register).

The 8087 also has temporary registers that it uses internally. and are 80-bit registers, along with two tag bits. However, is different: it doesn't have a sign, exponent, or tag. Moreover, the significand is 68 bits; has an additional bit to prevent overflow and three additional low-order bits for rounding, known as , , and .

In the microcode, each 16-bit micro-instruction performs one low-level operation. Many of the operations move data from one register to another. Other operations provide conditional jumps, subroutine calls, and returns.

The heart of the 8087's processing is the 69-bit integer adder, which I discussed here. (The adder has more than 64 bits because it has three rounding bits and a couple of additional high-order bits for overflow and multiplication.) Integer addition takes two micro-instructions. The first micro-instruction specifies the first argument to add and selects various options such as carry and rounding. (For subtraction, an option complements the second argument.) The second argument to the adder always comes from the register, which confusingly is unrelated to the register. The result of the addition operation is placed in a special register called the sum register. A second micro-instruction (which may be many instructions after the first) moves the result from the sum register to a destination.

Floating-point also makes extensive use of the bit shifter, which shifts a 68-bit value by an arbitrary number of positions, left or right; I wrote about it here. Like the adder, a bit shift operation takes two micro-instructions: the first moves a value to the shifter and configures the direction and amount of shift. The second micro-instruction moves the result from the shifter to a destination.

The addition/subtraction microcode

The 8087 implements almost all of its operations in microcode. The basic math operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) start by executing the same microcode (at decimal address . The microcode moves the two arguments into temporary registers and . Normally, these arguments are taken from the stack registers. The arguments can also be taken from memory, but I won't discuss that here.

Next, the microcode does a micro-subroutine call to handle the specific operation type. The 8087's microcode engine has a tiny ROM that holds a table of addresses, targets for microcode jumps or subroutine calls. Target 0 is special, however; it has three different addresses for multiplication, division, or addition/subtraction. (This is implemented by special-case circuitry in the ROM. When you're designing the chip, you can do weird, hacky optimizations like this if you want.)

The addition/subtraction micro-subroutine starts at address ; this microcode is shown below. The control flow is complicated, so I've put a flowchart in the footnotes. The microcode first handles the zero cases 0+0 or 0-0. Next, it subtracts the exponents of the two arguments. If the first argument has a smaller exponent (i.e., the result is negative), the arguments are swapped so the argument with the larger argument is first. (The 8087 keeps track of the sign of the result in the "sign latch"; if exchanging the arguments would change the sign, the latch is toggled at .)

#0232 jmp #0236 if not tmpA:tag ZERO 
#0233 jmp #0236 if not tmpB:tag ZERO
#0234 return if not unsigned sub 
#0235 jmp #0263            
#0236 tmpA sign -> sign latch

At address , the important alignment step takes place, shifting so the binary point lines up with . This is done by the microcode subroutine . The number of positions to shift is passed in the sum register; the difference between the two exponents was calculated in the previous subtraction. (If the difference was negative, it was complemented, so the value passed in is positive.)

Typically, the exponent of the result will be the same as the exponent of the (larger) value, but not always. Changes to the exponent are tracked in two places. First, a special two-bit register that I call the exponent adjustment () holds adjustments due to one-bit shifts left or right. The hardware initializes the register to 1 so there is room for a decrement. Larger exponent changes are tracked in the register's exponent field; the microcode initializes it to 0 at .

At address , the microcode makes a key decision: is the low-level operation unsigned addition or unsigned subtraction? Depending on the signs involved, the high-level operation (addition or subtraction) may not match the low-level operation. For example, for 2+3, -2-3, -2+(-3), and so forth, the two unsigned numbers are added; the result is 5, either positive or negative. But for -2+3, 2-3, 3-2, and so forth, the two unsigned numbers are subtracted; the result is 1, either positive or negative. I'll use "unsigned addition" to refer to the former cases, where the unsigned magnitudes are added, and "unsigned subtraction" to refer to the latter cases, where the unsigned magnitudes are subtracted. The key point is that an addition instruction may result in unsigned addition or subtraction, and the same with a subtraction instruction.

The 8087 has specialized circuitry to determine whether the low-level unsigned operation is addition or subtraction, allowing this to be tested with a conditional. The and values have sign bits of 1 for negative, 0 for positive. If you assign 1 to subtraction and 0 to addition, then yields 1 if the unsigned operation is subtraction and 0 if the unsigned operation is addition. The 8087 also has a conditional to test if the signs are the same or different.

Since the unsigned addition path is simpler, I'll start with it, at address . The steps are essentially the same as described earlier: aligning the numbers, adding them, and normalizing. First, the smaller number, in , is shifted right until the exponents match. Then the (unsigned) values are added. If there is a carry from the top bit, the result is shifted right at . Because the result is shifted right one bit, the special two-bit counter is incremented to track the required exponent adjustment.

At , the result's sign is updated with the value in the sign register. The 8087 supports three sizes of values: 80-bit temporary reals, 64-bit reals, or 32-bit reals. For the smaller sizes, the microcode subroutine trims the value to the appropriate size. (This is not as trivial as it sounds, since rounding up the result could require an adjustment to the result's exponent, recorded in the register.) Finally, the result's exponent is calculated from the initial exponent (in ), subtracting the adjustment value in 's exponent (normally 0), adding the adjustment value in the register, and subtracting 1 (because starts at 1). The exponent is stored in the result but also stored in the "exponent converter", a circuit that evaluates the exponent to detect overflow or underflow.

At this point, the addition/subtraction micro-subroutine returns to the common microcode. The common microcode checks if there was an overflow or underflow, indicating the value doesn't fit in a float. In this case, the subroutine is called to handle the value, which can involve triggering an interrupt, returning infinity, or returning zero. (For details, see my previous article.)

The result is pushed on the stack by writing it to the appropriate stack register. If the original instruction specified a stack pop at the end, the top of stack is marked empty, and the stack pointer is updated. Finally, the Run Next Instruction micro-instruction indicates the end of the microcode for the current instruction. The floating-point instruction has finally completed.

I'll switch now to the unsigned subtraction path, starting at . (Keep in mind that the instruction could be addition, for example, -2 + 3.) The microcode uses the 64-bit adder to perform an unsigned subtraction: ; the second argument is negated to perform subtraction. The result can be either positive or negative, depending on which value is larger. The rest of the path is the same as addition: setting the sign, adjusting the precision, and computing the final exponent.

If the subtraction result is zero, tests the three rounding bits. If a rounding bit is set, then the low bit of the result is set, and the exponent adjustment is decreased by 1 to counteract this. (For a denorm, the result is cleared since there's no "extra" room to promote the rounding bit.) There's a special path if the result is really zero, because the microcode needs to determine if the result is +0 or -0. Subtracting 0-0 joins into this code path to handle the various possibilities for adding or subtracting +0 and/or -0. Generally, positive and negative zeros work as you'd expect from a zero that "leans" one way. For instance, ⁺0 + ⁺0 is ⁺0 and ⁻0 - ⁺0 = ⁻0. But what if the zeros cancel? E.g. ⁺0 + ⁻0 or ⁻0 - ⁻0? In these cases, rounding down yields ⁻0 while the other rounding modes yield ⁺0.

The leading zero circuit counts the number of leading zeros to determine how much to shift. To keep the circuitry manageable, the leading zero shift is done in two steps. First, the result is shifted left by the number of leading zero bytes. Next, the leading zero circuitry counts the number of remaining leading zero bits, which will be 0 to 7 at this point. The result is shifted left by that many bits. The total shift amount is stored in 's exponent.

The unsigned subtraction path merges at with the unsigned addition path described earlier, adjusting the precision, computing the exponent, and storing the result. The micro-subroutine then returns to the common code that also handles multiplication and division.

Special-case handling in the common microcode

The 8087 handles many special cases for infinities, zeros, Not-a-Number, denormals, and other special values. The designers of the 8087 carefully thought about these special cases and attempted to handle them in mathematically reasonable ways. The table below is just part of the special cases that the 8087 handles.

Part of the special-case handling of infinities as described in the User's Manual.

While these special cases make the 8087 more accurate mathematically, they make the microcode much more complicated. The microcode below is common to addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. It loads arguments and stores the result as described above, but for the most part, it handles special cases. This microcode is "spaghetti code", with 18 conditional branches in a row to handle numerous special cases. I'll describe it at a high level here; the flowchart in the footnotes provides details.

#0001 call MEM_OP if mem op 
#0002 jmp #0004 if mem op
#0003 st(i) -> tmpB        
#0004 jmp #0018 if DE (denormalized) interrupt 
#0005 st(0) -> tmpA        
#0006 jmp #0008 if not reverse bit 
#0007 xchg tmp             
#0008 jmp #0019 if tmp anomalous 
#0009 call INSTR_SWITCH    
#0010 call NONNORMAL_RESULT if not exp normal 
#0011 jmp #0014 if dst st(i) 
#0012 tmpA -> st(0)

#0017 stackPtr++           
#0018 RNI
#0019 call SPECIAL_TMPS

#0021 jmp #0011 if expConv[0]

#0023 cond3b -> sign latch 
#0024 jmp #0039 if expConv[0]
#0025 jmp #0032 if not tmpB:tag ZERO
#0026 jmp #0035 if tmpA:tag ZERO
#0027 except:zero div

#0029 high bit -> tmpA:frac

#0064 jmp #0038

Looking at , the 8087 micro-architecture includes a conditional test that will check if either temporary register is empty or is tagged with a special value. If so, a subroutine that I call is called. It examines the two temporary registers and sets two flags to indicate what special handling needs to be done.

If both flags are set, one of the arguments was tagged empty, typically indicating a stack underflow. In this case, the microcode returns Not-a-Number (NaN). If the second flag is clear, then one of the arguments was a denormal number, a special value very close to zero. The arithmetic operation continues in that case.

The remaining code paths get complicated, for example, branching on the signs of the arguments, the specific arithmetic operation, or if an argument is zero or infinity. Eight code paths return Not-a-Number: n÷denorm, 0÷0, 0÷pseudo-zero, ∞×0, ∞÷∞, 0×∞, ∞ op ∞ proj, and ∞-∞ affine. Many of these are straightforward—0×∞ has no meaningful value, for instance—but the last two need a bit more explanation.

The 8087 has two different modes for infinity, selected by a bit in the control register. With "affine closure", infinity is signed, so +∞ and -∞ are two different values. The recommended mode is "projective closure", where infinity is unsigned. In affine mode, ∞+∞ is perfectly valid, yielding positive infinity. However, ∞-∞ is meaningless; an answer of 0 would be arbitrary, so NaN is returned. In projective mode, none of the operations on infinity make sense because infinity is both infinitely positive and infinitely negative.

The microcode has eight different paths to return infinity: n÷0, ∞×n, ∞×∞, n×∞, ∞÷x, x±∞, ∞±x, and ∞+∞ affine. (The first case assumes that the divide-by-zero exception has been masked.) For the first five cases, the microcode generates the sign for infinity by combining the signs of the arguments. However, the last three cases take the sign from the infinity argument and ignore the other sign. In other words, multiplication and division can flip the sign of an infinity, but addition and subtraction can't.

Two paths deal with special-case 0 results: 0÷denorm and n÷∞. The microcode generates 0 with the correct sign, based on the signs of the arguments.

The leading zeros circuitry

With subtraction, digits can cancel out, leaving leading zeros that need to be removed by shifting the value. The 8087's shifter can shift a 64-bit value by an arbitrary number of bits. The job of the leading-zero circuitry is to count the leading zeros to determine how much to shift. That is, it counts how many zeros are to the left of the first 1 bit and turns this into a binary value. This is basically the same as a priority encoder that encodes the position of the first 1 bit.

Leading-zero circuits are somewhat complicated because each binary output bit depends on all the input bits; a 64-bit detector has 64 bits coming in. One approach is to take the truth table and optimize it, ending up with a pile of logic. Another approach is to use a hierarchical approach, a tree with log(N) stages. The 8087 takes a simpler path: one pass to eliminate leading zeros a byte at a time, and a second pass to eliminate the remaining 0 to 7 leading zero bits. Each pass requires a separate 8-input leading zero detector circuit. This approach is slower, but the circuitry is much simpler: two 8-bit leading zero detectors instead of a 64-bit leading zero detector.

The schematic below shows the circuit that converts 0 to 7 leading zeros into a 3-digit binary value. To simplify the schematic, I've replaced the first layer of logic with a bitmask that represents the 8-bit input. For instance, indicates that the signal is high if the second bit is 0, the third bit is 1, and the remaining bits are arbitrary. I've added text descriptions; due to optimizations, the descriptions have some exceptions. For instance, matches anything with two leading zeros. It also matches some patterns with no leading zeros, but those don't change the result. The important thing is that it matches with 2 leading zeros and with 1 or 3 leading zeros.

The circuitry to detect 0 to 7 leading zero bits. The same approach is used to detect leading zero bytes.

The output from the circuit is a 3-bit binary value representing the number of leading zeros. The top NOR gate generates the low bit, set for 1, 3, 5, or 7 leading zeros. The high bit is generated by the bottom NOR gate: set for 4, 5, 6, or 7. The middle bit is trickier, with an additional layer of logic to determine if there are 4 or 5 leading zeros (or maybe 0 or 1). The two 1 cases block four zeros, while the 00 pair means that four leading zeros would turn into at least 6. (This is a hand-waving explanation, but one can enumerate the 256 cases and verify that they all produce the correct answer.)

To count the number of with leading zeros, similar logic is used. However, each group of 8 bits goes through an OR gate to detect if any bits are set in the byte. Thus, the logic determines how many bytes of leading zeros are present.

On the die, the leading zero logic is immediately to the left of the sum register, examining each bit of the sum register.

Most people don't give much thought to computer operations such as addition or subtraction. But there are interesting algorithms and special cases behind the scenes, and these features are embodied in clever silicon circuits. The intricate rules to handle positive and negative zeros, positive and negative infinities, and Not-a-Number are part of modern computers, since the 8087 led to the IEEE-754 floating-point standard used today. The 8087 went a bit overboard with special cases, however. Some 8087 features, such as projective infinity, unnormals, and pseudo-zero were dropped from the standard becauses they weren't worth the effort.

I plan to continue reverse-engineering the 8087 microcode; for updates, follow me on Bluesky (@righto.com), Mastodon (@), or RSS. I've been working on this with the members of the "Opcode Collective", especially Smartest Blob and Gloriouscow, who converted the ROM images to microcode data and extensively analyzed the contents. See the 8087 repository on GitHub for more. AI statement: Despite the presence of the em dash, no AI was used in the writing of this article (details). The Opcode Collective used an ML algorithm to classify each ROM cell to extract the microcode.

items.title: Java sealed classes and exhaustive pattern matching
items.author: hnisjafx40
items.content:
Java 17 introduced sealed classes, which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. For example, here’s a toy example using a sealed interface and records (inner classes are implicitly added to the permitted sub-types if an explicit list is not given):

public sealed interface SealedType {
    record TypeA() implements SealedType {}
    record TypeB() implements SealedType {}

    static SealedType of(String type) {
        return switch (type) {
            case “A” -> new TypeA();
            case “B” -> new TypeB();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        };
    }
}

If you are familiar with functional programming languages with algebraic datatypes, you can view this as similar to a datatype declaration in Haskell or ML:

data SealedType = TypeA | TypeB

We can then use this in a simple Main class:

void main(String[] args) {
    var val = SealedType.of(args[0]);
    System.out.println(switch (val) {
        case SealedType.TypeA() -> “A”;
        case SealedType.TypeB() -> “B”;
    });
}

OK, not so exciting. But one thing to note here is that we didn’t have to add a clause to the switch expression in our main method. This is because sealed classes (and enums) enable : the compiler knows exactly what the possible cases are, and so can check if you have covered them all. If you have, then you don’t need a clause. If you forget one (and don’t have a default clause), then you get a compile-time error.

This is great when you want to ensure that all uses of some type do cover all of the cases, but it does introduce a new type of breaking change: adding a new sub-type to a sealed class/interface may break consumers of that code. For example, adding a new case to our example will cause the main method to fail to compile due to the missing case. So if you export a sealed type in your API then adding a new subtype is a breaking change that would require a major version bump (if you’re following SemVer).

Compile-time or runtime error?

Although Java will produce a compile-time error for a non-exhaustive switch when you compile the consumer (main in this case), it cannot do so if the consumer is not recompiled when the sealed type changes. For example, suppose that we extend our SealedType with another case:

public sealed interface SealedType {
    record TypeA() implements SealedType {}
    record TypeB() implements SealedType {}
    record TypeC() implements SealedType {}

    static SealedType of(String type) {
        return switch (type) {
            case “A” -> new TypeA();
            case “B” -> new TypeB();
            case “C” -> new TypeC();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        };
    }
}

If we just recompiled SealedType.java and don’t recompile Main, then we end up with a if we trigger the new case:

Here we have the new MatchException being thrown. The Javadoc notes this potential issue with separate compilation, and also some corner-cases with nulls in patterns. So even if you were hoping that using sealed classes would statically ensure that you update all consumers when a new case is added, this is not the case unless you recompile everything.

I think for me the conclusion is that sealed types are probably most useful the implementation of a component, and are less useful when exposed in the public API that a component offers to other components (eg a library). For internal use, where you typically going to recompile everything together, you get the nice properties of exhaustiveness checking and higher compile-time safety guarantees. But when used across module boundaries, you may just be introducing new ways to break code, often only detectable at runtime.

(I discovered these subtleties when reviewing the preview support for PEM-encoded cryptographic objects, which makes exactly this mistake of baking a sealed interface into a public API and recommend clients to pattern match against that type. A predict a very high chance of breakage if they ever want to add a new case).

items.title: Dogs seem to agree with humans that 'bouba' is round and 'kiki' is spiky
items.author: gmays
items.content:
Picture a shape called 'Bouba'. What features does it have? Is it angular, rounded, soft, hard? What about a shape called 'Kiki'?

This fascinating psychological experiment was first conceived in the 1920s, and it suggests there may be something universal about the way we humans connect visual information, like shapes, with sounds.

Animal behaviorist Eleonora Biffi at the University of Parma in Italy led the research.

She and her team recruited 70 domestic dogs to participate in two almost identical experiments.

The first experiment involved 51 dogs and their owners. Each dog/owner pair entered a room set up with a screen and a speaker to the left, and another screen and speaker to the right.

After giving the dog an opportunity to explore the room and get settled in, the owner sat with them, facing the middle of the setup while the screens and speakers played.

Over roughly 15 minutes, the screens and speakers alternated through different combinations of a human saying either 'Bouba' or 'Kiki' over the speakers, and the two shapes above swapping between the left and right screens.

Meanwhile, a GoPro recorded each dog during the trials. The researchers later fed these videos into an AI designed to track where the dogs' heads were pointing, a stand-in for where they were looking, so they could check for any statistically significant patterns that might occur above random chance.

The second experiment, which involved 19 other dogs, was identical in design except that the owners wore headphones playing rock music to stop them from hearing the 'Bouba' and 'Kiki' sounds. The idea here was to remove any owner cues the dogs might have been following.

Overall, "dogs looked significantly more at the rounded shape while 'Bouba' was played, and they looked at and explored the spiky shape when 'Kiki' was played," Biffi and team report.

The main difference between the two experiments was that dogs in study 1 showed a general bias toward looking at the spiky shapes. That bias disappeared in study 2, when their owners were wearing headphones.

"It could be hypothesized that the dogs were influenced by the owners' unintentional cues. However, since humans typically show a stronger preference for rounded or curved shapes rather than spiky ones, this is unlikely," the authors write.

"Another possible explanation could be that, in the case of dogs, animals' facial configuration, especially when considering ancient dogs and wolves, is characterized by more angular, 'spiky' features, which contrasts with the round facial morphology typical of human infants and could plausibly contribute to an opposite bias."

There's still a lot more research to be done before scientists can definitively say dogs associate 'Bouba' with round shapes and 'Kiki' with sharp ones.

But these results are an interesting starting point for exploring bigger questions, like why dogs are quick to pick up on human language, and how they came to be our close companions in the first place.

The research has been published in .

items.title: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use
items.author: dom96
items.content:
Writing code is probably something LLMs have excelled at the most. But how much of their ability to write code is due to their understanding of it vs. just them recalling code snippets which were present in their training dataset or their context window?

This is what I set out to answer. In order to do so I decided to design and implement a programming language which, while usable for humans, should be as difficult for LLMs and coding agents as possible.

I figured testing an LLM’s ability to understand and write code in a programming language that it has never seen before was a good start. But I also wanted to include features in the language which exploit the weaknesses of LLMs. For example, their apparent difficulty in counting letters, their over eager safety guard rails and their keenness to follow prompts.

KillSwitch is an esoteric programming language which is designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents. It achieves this in many different ways, for example:

  • The language spec contains hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies. The spec also expects the human reader to deduce certain things, rather than having them explicitly explained.
  • Counting of letters in identifiers is a crucial aspect of the language, with the interpreter refusing to execute code which does not abide by rules based on character counts.
  • Certain constructs are designed to trigger the safety guardrails of the model, e.g. “hack into a computer”
  • “Ignore previous instructions” as a phrase which has meaning in the language aims to confuse the model
  • Scripts are mostly noise, being mostly composed of stories which can embed syntactically relevant instructions but which do not need to. Literals can be placed anywhere within a script and then referenced using line counts.

Fundamentally KillSwitch is a stack-based interpreted language with only a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements. So those aspects of it should be pretty familiar to any LLM (and human). One can definitely imagine creating a completely different programming language paradigm which could confuse LLMs even more. But as a first attempt, this seemed like a good approach.

The example above does not show a full KillSwitch script, but only a small snippet of it. It specifically shows how to push the string onto the stack. If you’d like to see a full Hello World example, check out https://killswitch-lang.org.

The interpreter and language specification of KillSwitch are open source and available on GitHub. Be sure to check them out if you want to learn more about the language.

So how successful is KillSwitch at preventing LLMs and coding agents from reading, writing and understanding it? I devised a set of tasks to find out. I benchmarked the major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against these tasks. The results are very interesting and provide a useful leaderboard for LLM models.

Claude’s Opus performs best, though it’s not Opus 5.5 but rather Opus 5 which does so. The difference doesn’t appear to be pure chance, Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models like Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon do poorly due to their overly sensitive safety guardrails. The best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro.

The best performing model scores a . So does this prove LLMs can “understand” the code? I would argue that the answer to this is “no”.

So far, the tasks given as part of these benchmarks are fairly simple. They feature the likes of “implement hello world”, “explain what this script will output” (for a script printing the max of two numbers), and “modify an existing script converting celsius to fahrenheit, to do the inverse conversion”. It is impressive that they can solve these tasks for a novel language that was built to confuse them, but it’s not a clear signal that they can understand the language. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder what an even more difficult language might show. For now I am eager to see how well soon-to-be-released models handle the current set of tasks, and if they do complete them all successfully, I do plan to devise another task set which is more complex.

If nothing else, it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks that are out there.

items.title: It's still ok to enjoy programming
items.author: goostavos
items.content:
Reading Hacker News makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming.

Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious.

To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point.

I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like Agda. There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun.

A few weekends ago: recursion schemes. Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas. But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why entire papers get written about Monoids. Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding.

I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.

It's OK to enjoy things. Doing so requires no economic justification.

  • [0] Take the time to understand one day. It is beautiful.
  • [1] I'm not there yet, but the goal of studying this is to give myself another tool for reasoning about program correctness algebraically (a topic I cover in my book!)

items.title: A skeptic's first contact with Kubernetes (2024)
items.author: pmoriarty
items.content:
I've been working on systems administration / engineering / infrastructure development for many years and somehow I've managed to avoid any interaction with Kubernetes. This avoidance wasn't accidental; my work required very tight control of workload placement in physical locations.

Over time, I developed a skeptical view of Kubernetes without really having a solid basis for it, other than a vague notion of it being "a new way of doing things" and "unnecessary complexity".

I decided it was time to base my opinions on facts rather than perception, so here I am, writing what I learned.

While there are a lot of tutorials covering the usage and operation of a Kubernetes cluster, along with basic descriptions of its components, they did not quite work for me. Many of these resources lightly cover the components do, but often miss the underlying reason or the tradeoffs.

This post aims to cover these concepts from a perspective I would've found useful, and it does not aim to be exhaustive.

Kubernetes allows you to run arbitrary workloads, and provides you with the ability to:

  • specify requirements (cpu, disk, memory, instance count, ..)
  • dynamically scale instance count

but the more important part, is what it for you:

  • picking which host an application runs on
  • "self-healing" (crashed instances get restarted, instances automatically moved out of faulty hosts)
  • exposes services for DNS-based discovery

and it only you to package your workload as a Docker image, which seems like a reasonable price to pay.

The basic building blocks that compose a cluster can be defined as follows:

  • Pod: a unit of work, consisting of a set of Docker images and their configuration
  • Node: a computer running the kubernetes node agent (kubelet). executes Pods.
  • Cluster; a logical collection of s along with the Control Plane.
  • Service: logical grouping of a set of pods
  • Namespace: a logical subdivision of the . provides scope for names (like DNS search domain)

It's easier to observe the relationship between these concepts in diagram form:

While this may be an OK explanation, it wasn't really something that would've been useful for me – a lot of infrastructure platforms look like this diagram; there's nothing special here

My opinion is that a large part of Kubernetes' value is derived from just two concepts:

A control loop will continuously perform (via a control element), if necessary, to achieve a , and it will do this by observing specific variables (via a sensor).

An interesting detail is that the control element does not necessarily affect what the sensor observes.

This description is very generic, so here are some examples:

  • A workload that needs to process events from a queue
    • Desired state: empty queue
    • Sensor: depth of the queue
    • Control Element: number of event processing servers
  • A workload that needs to horizontally scale to handle user load
    • Desired state: Maintain P90 latency below X ms
    • Sensor: Latency metrics from backend
    • Control Element: Spin up new Pods to handle the demand
  • Generic Health monitoring
    • Desired state: All Nodes are healthy
    • Sensor: Health metrics from nodes
    • Control Element: Remove Nodes from the cluster

A Service is a networking-level concept which provides stable access to a set of backing Pods, it offers:

  • A : unchanging (virtual) IP address & a DNS record
  • Load balancing: distributes incoming traffic across the Pods
  • Service discovery: allows other components to find and communicate with the Service

Compared to "classic" clusters, a Service provides a similar abstraction to the combination of:

  • N nodes running Keepalived + NGINX (with a dynamic set of backends)
  • CNAME records for the virtual (Keepalived) IP

Whenever a new Service is created:

  1. A Virtual IP will be assigned to it
  2. Every Node will update its networking configuration () to forward any packet destined to each Service's Virtual IP instead to the backing Pods.

The networking configuration is updated by a Controller that runs on every Node: kube-proxy, whose primary responsibility is to watch the state of all objects and update the rules on every change.

This design means that all Nodes act as load balancers for Service traffic, so there is no single point of failure in Service traffic forwarding, and that traffic forwarding capacity scales with Cluster size.

For me, an interesting property of this design is that every Node receives the rules for Service, which has some implications:

  • Very simple implementation for
  • The number of rules may be large, which may be problematic for certain traffic forwarding implementations ( linearly evaluates every rule)
  • Traffic is forwarded multiple times in some scenarios, providing higher availability at the cost of extra load on the cluster
    • When a Pod is moved to another node, the traffic will be forwarded twice until the old DNS entry expires
      • No need to deal with cache invalidation for DNS entries at the level
    • Misbehaving clients (eg: ones that do not re-resolve DNS before reconnecting) will continue to work

We can look at the life of a packet that travels from "Pod 1" to "Service 1":

or "how, when and where things run"

You can create a Pod manually, using a YAML definition like this one:

but by doing that, you are scheduling the execution of this pod ; which is easy, but has some nasty limitations:

  • If the Node that host the Pod dies, the Pod will not get re-scheduled
  • If the Pod is terminated due to resource pressure on the Node (via eviction) it also won't get re-scheduled
  • You can't go "now I want to have 2 of these"

Instead of creating a Pod directly, you can create a ReplicaSet which is a Controller, and as part of it's control loop it will ensure that the right number of Pod replicas are running at all times, which solves the problem of Node failure/eviction deleting your Pod.

ReplicaSets allow you to update the desired number of replicas, (eg: updating version, or exposing another port) – you would need to delete the resource and re-create it.

To address these limitations, you can use a Deployment, which is a Controller that will ensure the right number of Pods are running .

The part is very important, as Deployments allow you to update which image (or version) the Pod is running and to select the rate of change, covering the standard workflow of a "version upgrade".

Said differently, when you update a Deployment, it creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales it up while scaling down the old one, enabling rolling updates.

or "how data persists and moves with your Pods"

By default, containers within a Pod do not share storage/filesystem.

If you want to share storage between containers in a Pod, you can use an Ephemeral Volume, whose lifecycle is tied to the Pod - when the Pod shuts down, the data is deleted.

Ephemeral Volumes seemed useless, but they do have some use-cases:

  1. Log shipping from a sidecar
  2. A sidecar populating caches for the main application

If you want to have storage, you could use a Persistent Volume, which has a lifecycle that is decoupled from the Pod's.

You'd define such a Volume with a Claim, like this:

and you can then use it in a Pod like this:

Some things seemed interesting:

  • Multiple users (Pods) of the same Claim will share storage, as always this is fairly risky if there are multiple writers
  • A PersistentVolume is backed by different drivers (NFS, SMB, iSCSI, ..) but which one is being used is not clear to the Pod, so the Pod cannot rely on features (like atomic renames)

If you want to haver per-instance persistent storage, you can use a StatefulSet which defines in a single resource: a workload (Pod), replica count, mount configuration and volume claim .

Some interesting things with s:

  1. Pods have stable hostnames (, , ..)
  2. Deployments are executed in order:
    1. Creation of Pods in ascending order (0, 1, ..)
    2. Deletion of Pods in descending order (3, 2, ..)
    3. Updates Pods in descending order (3, 2, ..)

This seemed , and the explanations that I found online say that apparently lower numbered instances are "core" or "more stable" – I don't get it, as a crashy Pod will not get renumbered. Maybe it'd be better to update in descending "uptime" order? Maybe this "seniority"/"stability" got retconned for Pods, and Kubernetes just needed order?

Operationally, at this point it's still unclear to me how you'd manually investigate the contents of a Persistent Volume, other than attaching to the running container & executing commands there; what if my container does not bring a shell?

We've covered the main parts of Kubernetes - Control loops, Services, Workloads and Storage. Learning about this concepts has allowed me to form the less-baseless opinion I was looking for (though, I still have not operated or used a cluster).

Overall, I think the make a lot of sense, specifically I think Services (including the networking model, and kube-proxy) are fantastic, and that keeping the Controller pattern as an engine for resource management is the right way to operate.

I'm left with some open-ended questions/rants, which I'll leave here for your enjoyment

Your cluster could be changing at any point as work happens and control loops automatically fix failures. This means that, potentially, your cluster never reaches a stable state.

As long as the controllers for your cluster are running and able to make useful changes, it doesn't matter if the overall state is stable or not.

Why does it not matter if the state is unstable? If I'm operating a cluster that can't settle, I'd like to know immediately!

  • Given the Controller pattern, why isn't there support for "Cloud Native" architectures?
    • I would like to have a ReplicaSet which scales the based on some simple calculation for queue depth (eg: queue depth / 16 = # replicas)
    • Defining interfaces for these types of events (queue depth, open connections, response latency) would be great
  • Why are the storage and networking implementations "out of tree" (CNI / CSI)?
    • Assuming it's for "modularity" and "separation of concerns"
  • Given the above question, why is there explicit support for Cloud providers?
    • eg: LoadBalancer supports AWS/GCP/Azure/..

And for the largest open topic, even though this is not Kubernetes' fault, I have a rant I need to get out

The Kubernetes "community" seem to have absolutely hell-bent on making their lives harder by basing tools on of all things. It's like they saw Ansible and thought, "Hey, that looks terribly painful. Let's do that!".

Check out this RabbitMQ scaler (KEDA, maintained by Microsoft) as an example:

value: Message backlog or Publish/sec. rate to trigger on. (This value can be a float when mode: MessageRate)

What do you mean that the for depends on the of ?? And what do you mean is a string when it should be an enum??

How did Helm manage to become popular?? How is it possible for a tool like this to do of all things that could be done?

Take this arbitrary NGINX chart and check how most values are handled with manual string indentation:

Why are we generating a structured language (YAML), with a computer, by manually adding spaces to make the syntax valid? There should be no intermediate text-template representation like this one.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.author: pretext
items.content:
Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as —which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classicalalgorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum . These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2). 

In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.

These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.

A new reversible algorithm

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs. 

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

A hard first test: modular inversion

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself times, find . For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.

The memory demands of divsteps

Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer , find such that ≡ 1 (mod ). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called . Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.

Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called , is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.

How Claude got around the memory problem

Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).

Optimizing a quantum optimizer

Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.

When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.

A more efficient quantum decoder

The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position contains several acceptable values of . The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed-Solomon decoder.

Reed-Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a . The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.

Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed-Solomon decoding.

So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp-Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp-Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.

A simplified approach to storage

Switching to Berlekamp-Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.

Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones. 

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost. 

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.
