items.title: Rendering pretty sky in Around The World game
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
This post is part of a series about Around The World, a game of exploration and discovery at sea. The game is currently in early development. If you're new to this project, you can read up on it here.

In the last post, I got the game’s clouds to look passable. But after looking at it during playtesting, I still wasn’t satisfied with the way the overall picture of how sea, sky and clouds came together. With some small tweaks, things started to look a lot better.

Light scattering in clouds

I ended the previous post using a lookup table rendered out by povray, that contains the amount of light scattered out of clouds depending on light angle (horizontal axis) and cloud density (vertical axis):

And I wrote about my dissatisfaction with this table:

I am beginning to suspect that povray doesn’t actually simulate multiple scattering at all; the documentation does not say yes or no either way. No matter how many samples and intervals I configure, I can’t get the bottom of those spheres to become lighter.

Once again I’m tempted to write my own recursive ray tracer to confirm my suspicions, but I resisted the urge […]

In the end, curiosity got the better of me and I write my own multithreaded recursive Monte Carlo ray tracer in a few hundred lines of Rust. It’s extremely dumb and hard-coded for this specific situation, so it only renders one perfectly spherical cloud of uniform density. But it was enough to confirm that indeed, povray does not simulate multiple scattering. With multiple scattering, the lookup table looks very different:

The comparison is not entirely apples to apples, because I also tweaked some parameters and the scaling of the axes. But overall, the effect is clear: the light coming out of the cloud is distributed much more uniformly, making the cloud appear lighter overall.

At low density (thin clouds), the difference is not very apparent; the top rows of the lookup tables are very similar. After all, there isn’t much opportunity for a light ray to be scattered more than once when density is low. So let’s compare the look at a higher density, representing a thicker cloud layer. Here are some clouds rendered with the old LUT:

The “metallic” look that I mentioned in the last post is now gone; cloud bottoms are brighter, and lighting is smoother overall.

In reality, clouds aren’t just lit by the sun directly. They also receive, and scatter, indirect sunlight from the sky. Since this light is usually tinted blue, the clouds should take on a more blueish hue as well.

I don’t want to add a constant “blue” term, since that is only correct during daytime; we’d want clouds to follow the current colour of the sky even at sunrise, sunset or night. How could I do that in Godot?

The answer turns out to be simple, but requires some understanding of how Godot’s light rendering works. Besides direct light, which we already handle, Godot also takes into account indirect light from the environment. This all happens under the hood outside user control, so my understanding is vague, but good enough to be useful.

As far as I understand it, indirect light is sampled from a cube map or two, containing radiance and irradiance from every direction. (I know radiance and irradiance are different things, but I don’t fully understand the distinction.) For diffuse materials like clouds, I’d expect the this cube map (these cube maps?) to be sampled in the direction of the surface normal, since that represents where most indirect light is coming from.

At the bottom of clouds, this normal points downwards towards the ground, so the cloud is rendered with little indirect light here. In reality, it receive indirect light, but from above: it’s just scattered through the cloud. So, what would happen if we tweak the normal to point upwards to the sky instead? The effect is subtle but important; here’s before:

The clouds have indeed gotten a blueish hue, making them blend in with the sky much better, and generally giving them a softer and more distant look, as clouds should have. I like this a lot!

How about a sunset, when the sky is not almost uniformly blue? Here’s before:

The bottoms of the clouds are tinted orange, because the incoming direct sunlight is orange due to heavy Rayleigh outscattering. Here’s the same sunset with tweaked normals:

The clouds have turned pink! I think this is much closer to how real sunsets look; the pink hue is apparently the result of mixing red (direct sunlight) and blue (indirect sky light), with the green channel getting somewhat lost in between.

Another thing that bothered me was that the sky looked unnaturally yellow near the horizon. This is fine and expected when the sun is low, but it was happening even with the sun straight overhead, like here:

I suspected that this was due to applying too much outscattering during the raymarch compared to inscattering, so I tried various hacks like adding a fake multiple inscattering term. In the end, a better fix turned out to be changing the order in which operations happen during the ray march. Instead of:

  1. Add (blueish) light scattered into the ray segment
  2. Attenuate by outscattering over the ray segment (reddening)
  1. Attenuate by outscattering over the ray segment (reddening)
  2. Add (blueish) light scattered into the ray segment

The effect is that less attenuation happens along the way, compared to inscattering, and the result looks much better:

This should theoretically be an artifact of the numerical integration approach, and so the difference should disappear when increasing the number of integration steps. But it doesn’t, so I suspect there’s still something wrong somewhere. But it’ll do for now and hopefully forever.

To render a realistic sky, I have to use parameters of the real Earth, like atmospheric density, height and planet size. However, the planet in my game is about 75× smaller than Earth, and so it’s curved more strongly. So when we use Earth parameters for the sky, the sky’s horizon ends up above the actual horizon. In between the two horizons, the sky shader pretends that the atmospheric density continues to increase exponentially towards the centre of the planet, which causes a dark band that’s especially noticeable during sunrise and sunset:

To make the two horizons meet, I applied a simple hack to the sky shader: add a small value to the y (vertical) component of the global view vector, then re-normalize it. The effect is to pull down the entire sky, most strongly around the horizon, causing the dark band to disappear behind the horizon:

It’s a hack, but cheap and effective.

Ah, the bane of every modern 3D game artist. Games are rendered in HDR (high dynamic range) nowadays, meaning their colour values can go brighter than the maximum of 1.0. If we display these on a typical monitor, the result has to be clamped, resulting in patches of oversaturated colours:

To fix this, some formula is typically used to map the HDR values back into LDR space for display. Godot implements several tone mappers; I found Reinhard to be too dark, and ACES and AgX too desaturated. So in the end, I settled on Filmic tone mapper with a white point of 2.0:

It gives especially the clouds a nice soft look, and makes them fade into the distance much better.

The choice of white point is still fairly subtle since Godot itself recommends at least 6.0 for “photorealistic rendering”, but that just makes everything look darker.

Tuning the tone mapping is a tricky endeavour, because changes to the tone mapper affect everything that came before. So in practice, this process was not as linear as I wrote it down here, and required some back-and-forth between adjusting the tone mapper and the scene lighting. For one, I literally reduced the brightness of the sky by a factor of 2, which gave much better contrast after tone mapping.

If we want a proper day-night cycle, we need the sun to rise and set. And if we want our planet to feel Earth-like, the times of sunrise and sunset should depend on location and season. This dependence is due to the motion of the Earth around the sun and around its own axis. A similar thing happens with the motion of the moon through the sky, and the phases of the moon.

It seemed complicated to figure out all the math to do these calculations properly. So I took an easier route: I modelled the entire situation in the engine, making the planet and its moon spin around like in an orrery:

Then I let the engine figure out the inverse transformation to determine where things are in the sky, from the point of view of an observer somewhere on the planet’s surface. This worked well, and the rendered orrery turned out to be a useful debugging aid.

After all that, I think I owe you another sunrise video, don’t I? And let’s find a scenic in-game spot for it, too!

items.title: Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD
items.author: rs_rs_rs_rs_rs
items.content:
Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.

Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources, where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018, respectively.

We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with / / enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:

  • Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via , and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643.
  • Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl( (such as and ) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated.
  • Win the race condition using in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process.
  • Align IP socket allocations and set to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte . Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16.
  • Trigger the conditional out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields.
  • the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer.
  • Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.

That's the short of the matter, the longer version is more interesting, including the history of the vulnerability, as a short can be traced back ~37 years ago, in the original BSD sources.

Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a primitive, where the was caused by a , the was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass /, and the was a predictable kernel pointer location.

While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the and handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.

Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.

Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable or is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example implementation is here. FreeBSD and NetBSD have an implementation of safe-unlinking in their implementation.

Secondly, we can randomize the self-referential PTE map allocation address so that the targeted atomic decrement locations would not be possible. This is done by using a random byte () and selecting a PML4 slot (320 + (random_byte & 127)) at boot time, and installing the recursive entry at that location. The definition becomes a runtime expression, yielding bases from through at 512-GiB intervals. An example implementation is here. In case randomization is not suitable, other options might suffice, such as marking the PTE as read-only, and changing CR0.WP during modification.

Thirdly, the kernel allocator can be made non-deterministic using two approaches; by randomizing the base address where memory allocations occur at boot time, and additionally randomizing the allocation order at run time. The base address randomization is effectively free as the gap it creates can still be used later on; while runtime randomization does incur some overhead during allocation - it may be possible that more in-depth allocator changes could alleviate this impact. Either approach would be sufficient to break the predictable pointer location without additional vulnerabilities, be it software or hardware.

Furthermore, there are existing and upcoming compiler features that can be used to mitigate against entire vulnerabilities, from array bounds sanitizer (a subset of Undefined Behaviour sanitizer) which can eliminate out of bounds fixed size array accesses. Calif has suggested to FreeBSD that the array bounds sanitizer may make a useful exploit mitigation that can be enabled in release builds, along with privately reporting 21 issues that the array bounds sanitizer would have caught; some with local privilege escalation security impact. An upcoming compiler feature that can be used to help mitigate against heap issues is Alloc Tokens, which can be used to isolate pointer containing allocations from non-pointer allocations. This isolation can make overflows from the non-pointer containing allocation much more difficult to exploit by preventing pointer access, along with making vulnerability classes like Use-after-Free unable to use the opposite type of allocation as the replacement memory allocation.

Since its inception, OpenBSD has consistently championed proactive security through source code auditing, the replacement of insecure APIs, advanced password hashing, cryptography, privilege separation, sandboxing, along with memory safety via and ; frequently setting the standard for system and network hardening.

By proactively hardening, and adapting new and existing mitigation options, we can often systematically neutralize entire classes of exploitation primitives; or at the very least, increase the attacker's cost (i.e. additional time investment, additional vulnerabilities needed to exploit an issue, find alternative avenues, etc). Investing in defensive improvements before vulnerabilities are actively targeted raises the bar for attackers, helping ensure robust protection and long-term resilience. In the age of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, mitigating against entire vulnerability classes, combined with increasing attack complexity only becomes more critical.

items.title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
items.author: wawayanda
items.content:
print subscribers

I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.

My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.

Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.

Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.

The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.

Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.

In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.

Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.

When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.

Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and failed comprehensively for several centuries.

A key problem was that nobody on the Continent knew that porcelain was made from kaolin. Or that kaolinite alone didn’t actually contain enough glassy liquid silicate to make proper porcelain, so that Chinese potters added pulverized ‘China stone’ – a type of partly decomposed granite containing silicon – into the kaolinite.

Trying to make their wares porcelain-white, European potters added materials like tin oxide and ground glass to the clay, an approach that led to Italian maiolica, French faience, and Delftware. The results were often beautiful, but lacked porcelain’s impermeability to water, high tensile strength, and the distinctive ring made by porcelain cups when tapped with a spoon.

Enter Count Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus (1651–1708), a mathematician, physicist, and philosopher born in the Electorate of Saxony. Tschirnhaus initially studied math and philosophy but in his twenties became fascinated by porcelain. Beginning in about 1679, he conducted a series of experiments that used concave copper mirrors to beam intensely hot sunlight on multiple types of metals, minerals, and ceramics. Eventually he realized that glass lenses could outperform mirrors and invented a method of casting glass to make big, thick lenses for focusing sunlight, sending samples of the results to European monarchs in an unsuccessful quest to obtain financial backing to establish a science academy in Saxony.

In the winter of 1693–94, Tschirnhaus discovered a surprise: a type of clay that wouldn’t melt. Dug from Colditz, about 25 miles southeast of Leipzig, in Saxony, it contained kaolin (Tschirnhaus, of course, didn’t know this). Adding alabaster or chalk to the clay and heating the mix produced a hard, yellow, somewhat translucent ceramic that Tschirnhaus called ‘wax porcelain’. Unfortunately, he couldn’t produce it in quantity – his lenses could focus sunlight on an area of 10 to 15 square centimeters but not heat spaces of any size. When he tried making his porcelain in commercial kilns, their walls shattered or melted. Tschirnhaus was struggling to develop a better kiln when he was approached by Augustus the Strong, the ruler of Saxony.

Tschirnhaus, Böttger, and Gottfried Pabst von Ohain, a high-ranking mining official (in those days, the closest thing available to an earth scientist), developed a red clay that could be made into bricks suitable for porcelain kilns. In June 1708, Pabst von Ohain found a source of white clay – nearly pure kaolin, though he didn’t know it – and shipped it to the other two. Mixing the white clay with ground limestone and heating it in kilns made from the new red clay in August and September, Tschirnhaus single-handedly created a cup that looked and behaved very much like white Chinese porcelain.

He did not live to enjoy his triumph. In October, Tschirnhaus suddenly dropped dead, supposedly of dysentery. On his deathbed, he gave Pabst von Ohain a black box filled with documents. The box was found in Böttger’s belongings after his death, which may explain why he wrote to Augustus in March 1709, claiming to be the sole discoverer of the process to make porcelain. Augustus officially chartered the Royal Porcelain Manufacture in Meissen, another small town near Dresden, the following year and put Böttger in charge. It took ten more years for its workers to figure out that ‘China clay’ (or, more precisely, a similar local stone) was a better additive than limestone. Meissen then became Europe’s porcelain center. Augustus made so much money that he built a ‘Japanese palace’, filled it with Meissen copies of Asian originals, and crowed to visitors that he had beaten the Chinese – correctly, because Meissen porcelain was harder and less porous than the original.

If Meissen was Porcelain 2.0, the Dekton for my cooktop is Porcelain 3.0 or more. Made by baking a slurry of ground porcelain, glass, and quartz into slabs, running the slabs through a huge hydraulic press that applies 25,000 metric tons of pressure, and hardening them at 1,200 degrees centigrade, Dekton took six years and almost $200 million to invent. Traditional ceramics contain microscopic voids and flaws that act as ‘stress concentrators’, focusing rather than diffusing the energy from impacts, which is what causes them to crack. The high pressure and heat used to produce Dekton cause atoms in the particles of kaolinite and quartz to diffuse across the boundaries where they touch, turning the entire thing into what amounts to a single solid mass. In consequence, Dekton has nearly eliminated porcelain’s long-standing weakness: its brittleness and structural fragility.

Dekton is but one part of an ongoing resurgence in porcelain, which itself is part of the still larger revolution in materials science. The field was founded in the 1940s and 1950s, when physicists, chemists, and engineers had to work together in the Second World War, the Cold War, and the space race. But it really took off in the 1980s and 1990s, with the development of precision measuring and manufacturing techniques. Most of its innovations have been incremental, but the accumulated total has had enormous impact in our daily lives.

tens of thousands

Another personal example: My daughter, hit with a rare bone infection at age eleven, now has a porcelain hip joint – porcelain because the previous cobalt and chromium replacement joints can release metal ions into the bloodstream, which can migrate into the placenta of pregnant women, potentially harming the fetus. About the same time that ceramics firms introduced wet-activated tiles, researchers deployed 3D printing to create porous, lattice-like ‘bioceramic’ structures to replace defective bone. The structures are not permanent replacements but scaffolds that allow blood vessels and bone cells to migrate into the spaces in the bioceramic. Over time, the porcelain structure dissolves and is replaced by the patient’s own tissue. (The scaffold is expelled from the body.)

I could go on to talk about the use of nanotechnology to fill porcelain pores to enhance color depth and stain resistance, imprinting porcelain with silver ion layers to enhance antimicrobial activity, or the use of lithium disilicate to make ultrathin dental implants of unprecedented strength. But maybe the best way to say it is that my grandmother, who proudly displayed her mother’s eggshell-thin Meissen china on the sideboard, would have been astonished to find that I was cooking on a thin slab of porcelain, heedlessly dropping heavy pots of boiling water on its surface. But when I tried to explain how remarkable this is to my son, he gave me a blank look. He had never lived in a world that wasn’t made of porcelain.

Charles C Mann is a correspondent for

items.content:
Quick update here since a lot of folks asked about what slopcodebench is / where it fits in

Slop code bench is unique among benchmarks in that it makes a model work against a progressively disclosed list of features (checkpoints) that it doesn’t know it advance, inheriting the same codebase through the lifecycle of a single multi-checkpoint challenge

I like this because it much more mirrors how real software dev happens, rather than most benchmarks with one off tasks where slop code doesn’t hinder future progress

The original post[1] and the SOL/fable follow up[2] went into a bit more detail on the benchmark and its challenges

items.title: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware
items.author: ErenayDev
items.content:
After my mother passed away I ended up with a big box full of old film negatives containing photos from childhood family trips and similar. So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn’t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my Dell Camera controller app so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months.

Then I saw a post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already…..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named Negative Vibes, thought that was a cute name.

Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had a much improved situation with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready.

So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Writing a driver for undocumented hardware has always been tedious. You capture bus traffic, stare at hex dumps, and form hypotheses about what each register or control transfer does. You then test them one at a time, usually for weeks. None of it is conceptually hard, but it takes a lot of patience and skills.

That kind of work suits an AI model well. It can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice that a sequence repeats with one byte changing, and propose what that byte means. It can write the test to confirm it, and it doesn’t get bored. The human still decides what to build and checks that it works on real hardware, but the slog shrinks a lot.

Be aware that I did not use hw-harness in this form for my projects as this was basically bespoke code at that time, so this project is an attempt to make the harness more generic and shareable from the scripts I was using while doing the work. What hw-harness is meant to help your Claude or Codex session with:

1. Record a reference session. Run the vendor’s Windows driver in a KVM virtual machine, with the real device passed through to the guest. 2. Capture from outside the VM. Record the traffic on the Linux host with usbmon. It sits below the passthrough layer, so the guest can’t see it.

3. Repeat the same operation on Linux with your own driver, and capture that the same way.

4. Diff the two traces. Both come from the same instrument, so they compare directly. The differences are your list of driver bugs.

For devices with no bus to tap, such as an internal MIPI camera, the harness uses Windows-side inspection instead. That means INF files, registry data, ACPI tables and device properties.

The approach should be fine in the sense it doesn’t rely on copying any code instead it observes what the hardware does and only extract configuration data from the Windows drivers, so every constant in the new driver traces back to something recorded.

So for those interested I have 3 short descriptions of the projects I did and what was needed.

Comparing the driver output of two drivers available.

The first project is a SANE backend for the newer Plustek OpticFilm 8200i. It uses the Genesys GL128 controller (USB 07b3:1825) and had no Linux support. The older model with the same name uses a GL845 and is already handled by SANE.
  • Color, gray, infrared and color+infrared modes
  • Resolutions from 300 to 7200 dpi, at 8 or 16 bits per channel
  • Dust and scratch removal from the infrared channel
  • An exposure multiplier for dense negatives

It’s packaged as a Fedora RPM, built automatically on every push. I mostly tested it with my own Negative Vibes application as there are not that many options under Linux for negative scanning.

Upstream SANE’s genesys backend also gained support for this scanner in September 2026, so I compared the two. Both resolve the same fine detail at 3600 dpi. Mine is faster at full resolution (34.6 s against 54.4 s) and supports infrared dust removal. Upstream offers more resolution steps. The webpage has an interactive side-by-side comparison you can check out. These are single-unit, single-frame results, so treat them as one data point. Check out the interactive page I made showing the current state of the two drivers, hopefully the discoveries I made can be used by the SANE project to fix some smaller items in the upstream driver. Anyway, I put this project up more as a proof of concept due to that since I expect everyone including myself will use the upstream driver once it reaches parity with this one.

Full scan of negative completed including infrared cleaning of image.

A driver alone isn’t much use if scanning negatives is still painful, so I built Negative Vibes. It’s a GNOME app, written in Rust, for scanning colour and black-and-white negatives and slides on any film-capable SANE scanner.

The scan is kept exactly as the scanner delivered it: 16-bit, linear, with the infrared plane. Everything else is a stack of non-destructive settings on top, so you can change the look and export again. It includes:

  • Density-space negative inversion with film base and dye-crosstalk correction
  • Roll-wide settings with per-frame overrides
  • Infrared and software dust removal
  • IT8 calibration through ArgyllCMS
  • Export to TIFF, JPEG, PNG and DNG, with ICC profiles and metadata

It ships as a Flatpak that includes the scanner backend. It’s tested on the 8200i so far. The goal is to support any film scanner SANE supports. For that, SANE needs a standard way to expose infrared channels, which it doesn’t have yet.

Showing MIPI output before and after fixes. Colors are better than they look as I was sitting in a relatively dark room by the end of the session.

The camera in my Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 (Aura Edition) uses a Sony IMX471 sensor behind an Intel IPU7. On Linux it produced dark images with heavy vignetting and a strong yellow-green cast. mipi-fixes-x1-aura collects the fixes. It’s only relevant to this laptop, which is why it isn’t one of the bigger packaged projects, but I have already submitted the kernel patches to Kate Hsuan and the libcamera patches is being reviewed by Wim Taymans for submission to Libcamera.
  • A crop-selection bug returned an error before storing the crop rectangle, so libcamera assumed the full pixel array.
  • The test-pattern register was declared with the wrong width.
  • The analogue gain cap was too low, which cost about 1.8 stops of sensitivity.
  • Lens shading correction was missing entirely, leaving the corners about 2.7 stops darker.
  • White-balance statistics were summed at the sensor’s native bit depth against an 8-bit black level. That skewed white balance, and the fix applies to any RAW10/RAW12 sensor.

In a controlled low-light test, frame brightness rose from 31.1 to 90.9. The red/green and blue/green ratios moved from 0.890 and 0.672 to 1.047 and 0.823, close to a USB webcam reference. Blue is still about 17% short in low light, which I put down to grey-world white balance. Fedora 44 RPMs are on the releases page.

  • Reference captures are a big step. Having the AI compare a known-good trace against a failing one turns a vague “it doesn’t work” into a concrete list of differences. For example for the MIPI camera having a USB camera also connected so Claude could compare the two captures was critical.
  • The AI is good at the tedium. That covers decoding captures, writing probes and cross-checking constants. I still have to be the one holding the physical hardware.
  • Real hardware is the only judge. Every claim above was checked on the actual scanner or laptop.

If you have hardware with no Linux driver, try hw-harness. Thanks again to Glorious Eggroll for the inspiration.

NOTE: I am not claiming that my scans or MIPI camera is perfect now, but the scanner gives me decent looking scans and the MIPI camera looks a lot better than before. So over time I am sure we be able to tweak and polish further, but I am happy that it allowed me to move the needle despite lacking the in-depth knowledge for this type of work.

items.title: The engineering that allows articulated buses to bend
items.author: CharlesW
items.content:
Every day, countless people around the world board a bus to travel to a destination. These buses come in all shapes and sizes, from comfortable coaches to towering double-deckers. One of the best ways to increase a coach’s passenger capacity without adding height is to build the bus in at least two sections, adding a pivot point near the middle. The articulated bus is a common sight everywhere, but how they actually work, especially when they have a rear engine, is far more clever and interesting than you might think. A lot of these buses put brilliant engineering in plain sight.

America’s largest train museum, the Illinois Railway Museum (IRM), hosts a special event each year to celebrate the transit bus, one of the greatest forms of public transportation that does not ride on rails. IRM is home to America’s largest collection of preserved buses, and most of the over three dozen trolley buses and motor buses in the museum’s hands do run and drive. This vast collection makes IRM the only railroad museum in America with a regular bus service. You might think it’s weird for a train museum to preserve so many buses across three warehouse-sized barns, but buses and trains complement each other in functional public transportation systems. One helps the other.

I have not missed a single Bus Day since I started coming to the Illinois Railway Museum in 2022. This year’s Bus Day was the 11th running of the event, and in my experience, each Bus Day has been better than the last. This time, for example, there was a practical buffet of 13 buses to ride throughout the whole day.

One of those buses was King County Metro No. 4020, a 1987 MAN SG-T310 articulated trolley bus. This unit usually gets to stretch its legs on every Bus Day, and it’s a favorite among visitors because everyone loves a fun “bendy bus.” As my wife published posts about our Bus Day at IRM, some followers and readers asked a curious question: Just how do articulated buses actually work?

The answer to that question is more exciting than it would seem at first glance. Yes, a lot of bendy buses work exactly how you probably think they do. But others require quite a bit of clever engineering that you might not notice until after you read this.

Over A Century Of Bending

Let’s start at the beginning: the dawn of the articulated bus, because it’s important to see where we’ve come from before I show you where we are now.

The articulated bus came early on in the development of the transit bus. Some of the first known internal combustion buses were built in the mid-1890s, and while those units were small, they wouldn’t be for long. As technology progressed, builders figured out how to stuff more people in a single bus. This was great for efficiency. It was cheaper and more practical to stuff one bus full of people than it was to run multiple smaller buses. Mechanics had fewer buses to work on, the transit district had fewer drivers to hire, and there were fewer engines to fuel.

However, a rigid bus can only get so long before making it any longer leads to diminishing returns. Super-long buses can carry more people, but have a harder time navigating city streets. Building up may also not be possible, as a double-decker bus might interfere with overhead infrastructure or fail to fit into tunnels.

The solution was simple. Builders began assembling buses in two distinct sections. The second section of the bus would connect to the rear end of the coach’s front section through an articulating joint. The earliest example of an articulated bus I could find is this Dutch Ford Model T, which was built in the early 1920s. Check out how the interior of the rear section is paired with the front using an accordion-like central section:

This wasn’t the only way to do it. An even simpler method to increase bus capacity was to make a single-unit bus or truck tow a trailer that had seats in it. A good example of this type of bus is the Officine Meccaniche bus truck from 1930, which is pictured below.

The interior of the trailer was not connected to the main unit in any way. As a result, the trailer had its own entry doors. Often, buses like this had a conductor to signal to the driver when the bus was ready to get underway.

Of course, I cannot talk about towed buses without talking about the very fun trailer bus. Those weirdos are little more than tarted-up semi-trailers with seats and windows. But they aren’t really articulated buses, so I will talk about those buses on a different day.

Articulated bus history starts getting really interesting in the late 1930s. Over in Italy, Alfa Romeo produced the pioneering 1937 Alfa Romeo 110 AM-Macchi. This bus, which Curbside Classic said carried up to 180 seated and standing passengers, had a novel way of articulation. Unlike today’s articulated buses, which articulate horizontally and vertically like a trailer, the Alfa Romeo had only vertical articulation. Having the center section articulate up allowed the bus to drive up grades without getting stuck.

In 1938, the city of Baltimore put America’s first articulated bus into service. The Twin Coach Super-Twin was similar to the Alfa Romeo in that it articulated only vertically. To permit sharp turns, Twin Coach, like Alfa Romeo, designed a rear-wheel steering system. While extremely weird, there was some logic to this. Per Twin Coach, because its bus articulated only vertically, the bus floor is straight from front to rear.

The Twin Coach’s articulation was more of a transitional technology. After World War II, bus builders largely switched to the more modern articulation system that we know of today. Here’s America’s first fully articulated highway bus, the 1946 Kaiser built for the Santa Fe Trail Transportation Company.

How To Make A Bus Articulate

Today, there are generally four ways to achieve an articulated bus. Two concepts that I explained earlier, the trailer bus and the bus that tows a trailer, remain in operation today. Trailer buses can still be found in Cuba, and they’re glorious in their simplicity:

Meanwhile, over in Munich, Germany, the Münchner Verkehrsgesellschaft runs the Busanhänger (bus train), which is a bus that tows a separate trailer that is also a bus. These were built in just 2022 by Sono Motors:

Here in America, you’ll generally find two kinds of articulated buses. The first, and older type, is the puller. In puller designs, the front section of the bus is a complete vehicle. The engine will usually be located towards the rear of the front section and under the floor. Only the rearmost axle of the front section (typically the middle axle of the whole bus) is powered.

Built from 1980 to 1986, these buses feature a Cummins 855 cubic-inch NHHTC straight-six mounted under the floor near the middle axle of the bus. That engine drives the middle wheels through either an Allison HT740 automatic or a Voith D864.2 automatic, both featuring four speeds.

Puller buses usually connect to their rear sections through a somewhat complex articulation joint.

This unit consists of a front and rear subframe that connect to the front section and the rear section, respectively. They meet in the middle, where they ride on a ring of bearings. These bearings allow the front and rear sections to turn relative to each other. In other words, it functions like a joint. In a puller configuration, the rear section of the bus straightens itself out as the front section pulls the bus forward. It’s like a semi-truck trailer, but with a few extra steps. These joints tend to be made out of materials like welded steel or cast iron.

From here, a bus builder will place a turntable on top of the articulation joint, bellows to seal the bending path between the two bus sections, and flexible cabling to provide power to the rear of the bus.

The benefit of the puller bus is that it’s technically a simpler design. The rearmost axle isn’t powered, and the articulation joint needs fewer components to get its job done. Anecdotally, some bus drivers I’ve spoken to prefer puller buses in snowy situations, since the powered axle is ahead of the articulation joint. Articulated buses also have a limited amount of vertical flexibility, permitting them to climb city streets.

However, puller-type articulated buses have one main drawback, and it’s that, generally, the floor cannot be lower than the engine that lives right in the middle of the bus. Some puller-type articulated buses manage to have a low floor by moving the engine to a side of the bus and having the lower floor go around the engine.

The Van Hool AG300 has this design, and while it has a low floor, the large engine takes up a vast amount of space that could be used for seating. Check it out:

How A Rear-Engine Articulated Bus Works

The preferred solution to this problem is to place the engine at the very rear of the bus, where it won’t gobble up valuable passenger volume. Yes, a rear-engine bendy bus!

Here’s where the engineering gets really fun. In a rear-engine articulated bus, the front section of the bus now becomes the “trailer,” and the powered rear section of the bus pushes the whole bus forward. Transit departments all across America have buses like this, and you’ve likely ridden on at least one. You can usually tell that you’re on a rear-engine articulated bus because you’ll find the engine’s exhaust and vents right there at the rear.

If you’re experienced in towing a trailer of any kind, you know that having the trailer overpower the tow vehicle is a bad idea. That’s a great way to jackknife your whole rig. Yet, articulated transit buses easily glide through their cities without crumpling into an L-shaped mess.

How rear-engine articulated buses achieve this has a lot to do with the articulation joint. Much of the core design of a pusher bus articulated joint is the same. You still have the two plates meeting at a circular bearing in the middle. But now, there’s more.

One of the biggest additions to the articulation joint of a pusher bus is a set of dampers. The dampers provide hydraulic resistance, slowing down the rotation speed of the sections. Newer joint designs feature semi-active dampers that utilize an array of sensors and a control unit. The bus tracks its speed, steering angle, and articulation angle.

If the control unit detects that the bus might become unstable, the dampers can become firmer to further restrict movement. If the control unit fails, the articulation joint still has passive damping, and if the driver turns sharply enough, there are bump stops at the end of the articulation joint’s travel. Likewise, the articulation system can work in tandem with the drive-by-wire system to cut throttle when things are getting a bit too spicy. Having the active system allows the joint to be stiff during high-speed driving, and more relaxed in low-speed cornering.

Here’s an example of how a HÜBNER system intervenes based on bending angle:

Pusher buses then use similar copolymer-based bellows and flexible power systems as a puller bus does. Some of these systems are designed to be universal, so they could be installed on just about any articulated bus, no matter if it’s a diesel, a hybrid, natural gas, electric, hydrogen, or something else.

There are even articulated buses out there that have two articulation joints, essentially creating a long snake of a three-section unit. These buses (example below) tend to be rare and are often used more like trackless trams, as their sheer length limits their maneuverability.

As for how driving an articulated bus is different from a rigid bus, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority has a neat video explainer from a driver (click here if you do not see the embed):

A lot of this technology has been around for a long time. HÜBNER says it’s been making articulated bus bellows since 1952. JOST, another German maker of commercial vehicle parts, says it made its first ball bearing turntables in 1952.

Meanwhile, FG Fahrzeugwerkstätten Falkenried GmbH claims to have invented the damper system for today’s low-floor articulated buses in 1975. One of the first rear-engine articulated buses to use this technology was the 1978 Mercedes-Benz O 305 G:

All of this history and engineering is essentially hiding in plain sight, or right under your feet. When you’re riding these buses, you can’t see the articulation joint hard at work to keep the bus comfortable and under control. You might not have even noticed that many “bendy” buses have rear-mounted powertrains.

For decades, the articulated bus has proven itself to be the right kind of bus for when a transit district wants to increase available passenger volume but without deploying more buses. Articulated buses also work on the routes where a tall double-decker bus just won’t work. Of course, they’re also a subject of curiosity for transit enthusiasts, too.

The next time you’re on a bus during your morning commute, think about the century of advancements that led to that bus ride. It all started with wooden carriages slowly getting people to their destinations. Now, the buses of today are marvels. Also, be sure to thank your bus driver and the mechanics, because without them, your commute wouldn’t go nearly as smoothly as it does.

items.author: vishnukool
items.content:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.

You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo

We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.

One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.

Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.

Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:

* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.

* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.

* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.

* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.

We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.

Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.

I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.

If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.

Thanks!

items.title: Launch HN: Magnitude (YC S25) – Self-optimizing inference engine for agents
items.author: anerli
items.content:
Hey HN, Anders and Tom here. We're building Magnitude, an inference engine for agents that optimizes itself to run as fast as possible on your hardware. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows on any hardware and is up to 2x faster than llama.cpp.

We're both software engineers and previously built an open source browser agent to 4k+ GH stars and 100k+ downloads. We increasingly wanted to run it on local models, but found that no inference engine worked for our use case.

Inference engines today all make a performance tradeoff. They are either:

- Built for batched inference on datacenter hardware at the cost of single-session performance (vLLM, SGLang) - Designed for broad compatibility instead of optimizing for specific hardware (llama.cpp, Ollama) - Specialized for specific hardware or models but lacking engine completeness (oMLX, ds4)

Plus none of them are designed for running agents locally. Sessions are long, several often run at once, and you still want to use your computer for other things.

Magnitude is built for maximum performance on your hardware and running local agents:

- On-device compilation and tuning: Kernels are written with flexible parameters that are tuned on your actual device before the model runs. This gives you broad hardware compatibility with the same performance ceiling as hardware-specific kernels.

- Focus on best architectures: We write our tunable, highly efficient kernels for the most popular open-weights families. This allows us to achieve and surpass the performance of hardware or model specialized engines, without forcing ourselves to over-generalize at the cost of performance.

- Dynamic memory allocation: Magnitude reserves only enough memory up front to hold model weights. As your agent sessions grow, the memory heap dynamically increases, and frees itself when agents stop. Your hardware can still be used for other stuff while agents run.

- Hybrid paged attention: We borrow the best ideas from engines like SGLang to allow concurrent sessions to share prefix caches, but optimize placement for memory-adjacency so single-session performance doesn't suffer.

Magnitude is fully open source (Apache 2.0). We built it in Rust, including a custom GPU kernel runtime and autotuner. We take inspiration from the best innovations in inference from academics (e.g. FlashAttention, FlashInfer, TurboQuant) as well as other engines (e.g. SGLang radix attention) to reach the performance ceiling.

Benchmarked against llama.cpp with Qwen 3.6 35B A3B (4 bit), 64k context, no speculative decoding:

Metal (Mac M4 Pro 48 GB) - 92% faster decode (30 tok/s → 57 tok/s) - 9% faster prefill (466 tok/s → 507 tok/s) - 28% less per-agent memory usage

CUDA (DGX Spark) - 19% faster decode (49 tok/s → 58 tok/s) - 23% faster prefill (2,033 tok/s → 2,507 tok/s) - 27% less per-agent memory usage

Magnitude ships as a desktop app that you can easily connect with whatever agents you already use (Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, Codex, and more). It automatically runs models on demand when these agents actually need them, and shuts them down after inactivity. Here's what it looks like: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qE8BWEZu7o

We're excited to push Magnitude further to let you run bigger models on the same hardware while continuing to improve performance. Our plans include:

- Expert streaming: store experts on RAM or disk and load them just-in-time. This lets you run models bigger than what otherwise would fit on your GPU.

- Kernel compiler: our current kernels tune a few parameters to fit your hardware. We can take this further with a fully custom compiler that automatically chooses how to fuse kernels and which implementations to use, to make it fit to your hardware even better.

- Multi-device utilization: Make the best possible use of all hardware on a system (CPU, GPUs, RAM, disk) by detecting these and automatically solving for the best model layout.

We'd love for more people to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we'll be around all day!

items.content:
The following explanation is taken from https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49622607:

Alan Kay performs an improvisational avant garde layered audio feedback loop about Claude Shannon, live online during Kristen Nygaard's 100-year birthday celebration.

Alan was scheduled to talk about how encountering Simula sparked his early thoughts about objects. During setup, somebody had the live stream playing out loud near an open Zoom mic, so his own voice kept arriving back in his ears about 21 seconds late, over and over.

What he said was not random: "Shannon gave us a way of dealing with noisy channels." And: "I think about that almost every day. I realize what the fuck is going on and it's just so amazing." Shannon's noisy channel coding theorem is the math for exactly the kind of channel that was garbling him as he praised it.

Alan joked it was "being rerouted to Mars and back." At the speed of light, a 21 second round trip is about 3 million km one way -- eight trips to the Moon and back, but only about a seventeenth of the way to Mars at closest approach.

This is an accidental Zoom performance of Alvin Lucier's "I Am Sitting in a Room" (1969), where Lucier re-recorded his own voice in a room until only the room's resonance remained. Here what remains is the network: delay, compression, dropouts.

Bonus noise: YouTube's auto-transcript bleeps Alan's enthusiasm into [ __ ]. So the full chain is: Alan's voice, Zoom, stream, room, Zoom again times three, my screen recording, YouTube's speech recognizer, a censored transcript.

The fix: "Just turn off the audio at your end on Zoom."
